The observation of a difference in the lifetimes of B^0_s mesons and B^0 mesons has been a key factor in scrutinizing theories beyond the Standard Model. Accurate measurements depend heavily on sophisticated detector systems, particularly those featuring precise momentum measurement tools. Within the ALICE experiment at the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the Central Electric Barrel Detector was developed to meet the high requirements for tracking charged particles in beauty quark decay processes. This detector system, with 40 narrow, segmented electrodes forming its barrel section, was specifically designed to provide excellent spatial resolution and allow for the precise measurement of beauty quark decay modes, such as the D_s^+- and Lambda_c^+ particles, which are critical for obtaining accurate B^0_s and B^0 meson lifetime differences. The design, construction, and performance of the Central Electric Barrel Detector have been detailed, including the development of a new readout system on a Custom LSI and the calculation of the detector's resolution based on geometric and material considerations. Experimental confirmation of the predicted performance has been obtained through beam tests at the SPS and in the ALICE experiment during beauty quark production periods. The Central Electric Barrel Detector has been an integral part of the ALICE experiment and has enabled the measurement of rare beauty quark decay processes, including those involving the D_s^+- and Lambda_c^+ particles, which have contributed significantly to the establishment of world-best measurements for the branching ratios of these processes and have further refined the understanding of beauty quark hadronization by identifying rare decay modes of beauty hadrons. The design of the detector has also been applied to the development of a proposed future beauty quark experiment at the LHC. The research detailed in this thesis has contributed to the following advancements in beauty quark physics: the most precise measurement of the D_s^+- lifetime; the first measurement of the Lambda_c^+ lifetime; the establishment of world-best measurements for the branching ratios of the D_s^+-->f_1(592)(eta') and Lambda_c^+->Lambda K^0_S processes; and the development of a proposed future beauty quark experiment at the LHC. The findings have been published in the following research papers: JHEP 01 (2022) 156; PRL 129 (2022) 092001; PRL 129 (2022) 242002; PRL 129 (2022) 242003; PRC 105 (2022) 094

The key aspect of this approach is the analysis of the convergence of the numerical scheme. Under certain conditions, it is possible to establish the convergence of the controlled process and the associated cost functional. A key finding is that the rate of this convergence can be determined and it is shown to be more precise than previously established rates. A comprehensive analysis of the anisotropic properties of particle flows has been performed utilizing LHC data, focusing on the interpretation of flow fluctuations within the quark-gluon plasma. An improved approach to characterize anisotropic flows is introduced and applied to the analysis of ALICE, ATLAS, and CMS data sets. Results from this analysis support previous findings, indicating that the anisotropic flows are influenced by the anisotropic densities and viscosities of the quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, an investigation of the correlations between flow fluctuations and the anisotropic densities and viscosities of the quark-gluon plasma is conducted. This analysis demonstrates that the anisotropic viscosities of the quark-gluon plasma exhibit a non-trivial connection with flow fluctuations, whereas the anisotropic densities of the quark-gluon plasma exhibit no such connection. A proposal for utilizing entropy densities to characterize the anisotropic properties of the quark-gluon plasma is also presented. A critical assessment of previously proposed approaches to characterize anisotropic flows is provided, along with a discussion of the implications of the analysis for the development of relativistic hydrodynamic models. This analysis has far-reaching implications for the study of fluid dynamics in relativistic physics. A key outcome is the identification of flow fluctuations as sensitive probes of the anisotropic viscosities of the quark-gluon plasma, offering valuable insights for theoretical models seeking to reproduce experimental data. This analysis has significant value for current and future heavy-ion collision experiments seeking to advance the understanding of relativistic hydrodynamics in physics. A supplementary analysis of the anisotropic properties of particle flows in proton-proton collisions is also conducted, yielding valuable information about the anisotropic properties of hadronic interactions and providing a critical baseline for heavy-ion collision experiments. This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model to analyze non-linear and time-varying components in count time series data. The proposed model specifically addresses two significant challenges faced by traditional Poisson models: (1) nonlinear dynamics and (2) structural breaks. We achieve this through the use of natural exponential functions and trigonometric terms, as well as a varying coefficient approach, all combined within a Bayesian framework. The model's parameters are proven to be identifiable and we develop a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to estimate the model's values. The effectiveness and applicability of TV-PARX are demonstrated through simulated and real-world data examples, showing its capabilities in accurately capturing non-linear and time-varying components, even in data with significant structural breaks. The results highlight TV-PARX's superior performance when compared to its main competitors, including the Time-Varying Poisson ARMA and Bayesian Poisson regression models. Neural Descriptor Fields, a novel framework consisting of a set of neural networks that generate detailed object representations, are leveraged to develop a key technique for teaching robots new tasks using only a few examples. In tasks like object manipulation, where actions are guided by subtle differences in object features, this method helps reduce the necessity for numerous demonstrations. By teaching a set of Neural Descriptor Fields to replicate the characteristics of objects shown during training, it enables the automatic discovery of distinct features that define tasks and objects. When applied to a task, it identifies the specific object features necessary for action success, thereby cutting down the required demonstrations by up to 90%. The benefits of Neural Descriptor Fields are demonstrated across five manipulation tasks in simulated and real-world settings, along with three human-robot interaction tasks in a real-world setting. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/PRPR-Lab/NDF_TRA.

We present a novel approach where wide-field photometry helps determine the vertical aerosol optical depth without the need for absolutely calibrated luminosity measurements. Traditional methods for deriving aerosol optical depth rely on calibrated solar photometry with narrow field-of-view measurements. However, photometric data sets with wider fields of view are more common and can be used to determine aerosol optical depth at lower elevations. We explain how the variation in count rates with solar elevation can be used to determine aerosol optical depth with no need for absolute calibration. We apply this technique to SCIAMACHY/GOME-2A data sets from the ESA's Environmental Sentinel-4 precursor mission, derived from raw data through the full retrieval chain, and compare them with directly measured values from AERONET ground stations in Europe. Although differences are generally small, we find that SCIAMACHY's larger field of view results in slightly higher estimates of aerosol optical depth at low elevations. We propose this technique as a means of recovering aerosol optical depth from legacy and future spaceborne missions with wide field of view measurements, and from ground-based measurements with large field of view instruments deployed in different locations. We also suggest it as an easy way to process data sets from existing platforms before comparing them with values from AERONET ground stations. We demonstrate the applicability of this technique to simulated OECO Sentinel-5 precursors with a field of view similar to SCIAMACHY's but with improved spatial resolution. Accurate object pose estimation in complex real-world scenarios is a difficult task, largely because it involves projecting objects that can be partially hidden from the point cloud represented by a LiDAR sensor. Current techniques that estimate object pose from point clouds rely heavily on 3D distance metrics, making them less effective when the target object overlaps with the surrounding environment. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel technique called projection grouping, which aggregates point cloud projections based on a proposed similarity measure, in order to reduce the impact of overlapping projections. By simplifying the problem to a 2D image representation, we leverage conventional 2D R-CNN object detection, incorporating a proposed class-aware IoU metric to enhance performance. Through rigorous testing, our technique demonstrates a substantial improvement in pose estimation accuracy when the target object significantly overlaps with its surrounding environment, as validated by LiDAR-based pose estimation benchmarks in indoor and outdoor scenarios. Furthermore, our technique has the added benefit of producing bounding box predictions from the point cloud, enabling real-world applications in robotics, among others. The code for our technique is publicly accessible at this link https://github.com/zhengyun113/pgmrcnn.

Research focused on an aluminum alloy object with a length of 50mm, a width of 20mm, and a thickness of 2mm, struck the bottom of a still body of water with a speed of 4.5m/s. High-speed images captured at 50000 frames per second and analysis of pressure sensors with a 1kHz sampling rate helped analyze the dynamics of the surface seal. Deformation of the object was also simulated using finite element methods. Results showed that the pressure reduction inside the cavity increased with impact speed but the rate of this increase slowed down. The pressure reduction was found to accelerate over time but this acceleration decreased with impact speed. The time required to reach the maximum pressure also increased with impact speed. The shape of the pressure curve changed with impact speed but this was not observed for the pressure range of 1 to 10 MPa. The pressure seal occurred in the same time period as the object's rebound but this was found to decrease with impact speed. The pressure reduction was found to be related to the object's deformation but the rate of this deformation slowed down with impact speed. The time required for the pressure to return to zero also increased with impact speed. We introduce a novel variational approach that generates a compact representation of polymers based on their molecular structure. This method utilizes a special type of neural network called a graph neural network to create a simplified model of polymers, which consists of a few representative monomers and the bonds that connect them. We have developed this variational approach to better infer the properties of polymers in complex liquids by reducing the complexity of molecular structures. Unlike previous methods that focus solely on the most probable conformation of polymers, our approach takes into account the variability of molecular structures by modeling the distribution of all possible conformations. We have put this method to the test on simulations of melt liquids consisting of polyethylene chains and have found that it accurately predicts the Guay-James overlap distribution and the distribution of end-to-end distances in polymer chains. Furthermore, this method can be applied to a wide range of polymer systems and melt liquids consisting of Lennard-Jones beads. The code for this method is an extension of the HOOMD-blue molecular dynamics simulation software and is an open-source platform. The new method we have developed demonstrates a significant improvement over existing approaches, showing a 2.5 times increase in the accuracy of its predictions for the Guay-James overlap distribution and a 1.5 times increase in the accuracy of its predictions for the distribution of end-to-end distances when compared to the most probable conformation of polymer chains. The code for this method is an extension of the HOOMD-blue molecular dynamics simulation software and the changes we made are an important contribution to the development of the software. The new variational approach we have developed can be an invaluable tool for inferring the properties of complex molecular systems by representing the distribution of their conformations. In recent years, attention mechanisms and convolutional neural networks have significantly improved image segmentation, particularly for medical images. To further enhance segmentation, we propose the Dilated Dense Attention Unet, a model that incorporates both attention and dense connections in a streamlined architecture. The purpose of this model is in the segmentation of esophageal tumors from endoscopic video frames, though its benefits can be applied to other medical image segmentation tasks. The proposed model consists of two main components: a feature extraction block utilizing dense attention to focus on high-detail, clinically-relevant information and a decoder block employing dilated convolutional neural networks for efficient upsampling. Experimental results on the ESOP-ET dataset demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model over baseline models, with an overall improvement of 10.5% in Dice similarity index and 12.6% in categorical Dice similarity index. The model's efficiency is highlighted by a significant reduction of 91.4% in memory usage and 1.5 times faster computation compared to its closest competitor. In diverse societies where multiple languages are spoken, NLP research can significantly enhance everyday life by developing effective, widely-used systems, despite significant obstacles hindering universal language understanding. This PhD project focuses on exploring essential aspects of a unified, pervasive NLP framework, delving into both theoretical knowledge and practical applications that can benefit multilingual communities. The study demonstrates the feasibility of training high-performance neural language models on mixed-language data, discovers key differences in language usage patterns, and develops a pioneering, universally applicable machine translation approach that leverages implicit knowledge. Furthermore, the research establishes a threshold for assessing paragraph similarity and creates an innovative, hybrid text generation model. The findings and methodologies developed throughout this project have been thoroughly tested and validated, with results demonstrated on six languages. The analytical techniques and innovative solutions presented here can serve as a foundation for ongoing challenges in NLP, particularly those related to unified representations and language similarity analysis. The project's outcomes also include a comprehensive, open-source software package, the JMDT framework, which encompasses all developed models, assessment tools, and supporting code, enabling the reproducibility of research findings and facilitating the integration of the project into ongoing NLP research efforts. The impact of this project is far-reaching, with potential applications in areas like language teaching, cultural exchange, and emergency translation services, among others. The JMDT framework and the research data used throughout this project are both publicly accessible, with the software package available under the Apache License 2.0 and the data released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. The project's findings have been tested on languages from diverse language families, encompassing languages with complex writing systems, tonal languages, and languages with significant dialectal variations, thereby demonstrating the broad utility of the solutions developed. The project's outcomes can be utilized in real-world contexts, such as developing a unified NLP framework for languages within a single society, combining languages that share a common grammar or syntax, or integrating languages that serve as dialects of a single language. The project's innovative solutions, coupled with the publicly available software and data, set a significant milestone in the development of a unified NLP framework for diverse languages, thereby contributing to the advancement of NLP in multilingual societies. The project's name, JMDT, is an acronym for Joint Multilingual Document Translation. Calculating energy loss functions for tantalum oxides is complicated due to the presence of local field effects and spin-orbit coupling, which can't be ignored in these systems. Using a method that incorporates the specific crystallographic structure of each oxide, we determined the energy loss function for a range of tantalum oxides, including taO, ta$_2$O, taO$_2$, ta$_2$O$_3$, taO$_5$, and ta$_2$O$_9$. The energy loss function, which indicates the tendency of an electron to interact with a photon and change its energy, was computed across various binding energy ranges. The resulting data shows that the energy loss function exhibits distinct patterns in response to changes in both the oxygen content and the presence of vacancies, and can potentially be used to guide experimental studies of these oxides via X-ray absorption near edges structure and X-ray photoemission spectroscopy. The computed energy loss functions also demonstrate minimal variation with respect to different crystallographic phases, suggesting that the energy loss function can serve as a reliable indicator of a tantalum oxide's chemical composition, even in scenarios where the crystal structure remains unclear. The associated code is available publicly and can be utilized to calculate energy loss functions for other materials by inputting the corresponding crystallographic data. The energy loss functions for the computed tantalum oxides are deposited in the Materials Expression Online System as MaterialX documents. The experiments behind this paper were conducted using the Advanced Photon Source at the Argonne National Laboratory, a U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science User Facility that is operated by the University of Chicago. The growing physical and social segregation of communities, as described by Bill Bishop in "The Big Sort," has significant implications for the dissemination of false information on the internet. This study suggests that, because people with diverse viewpoints tend to live separately from one another, they are less likely to interact with opposing perspectives online and are therefore more likely to engage with the spread of misinformation. We have developed a mathematical model that takes into account the ideas of "The Big Sort" and the characteristics of users who diffuse false information, and has been tested using data from an online platform. This research demonstrates that more intense physical and social segregation accelerates the dissemination of false information and enhances the durability of its spread, whereas interventions that promote social mixing, increase the diversity of online interactions, or raise the cost of spreading false information can slow the spread of misinformation. This model has been applied to evaluate the impact of "The Big Sort" on the diffusion of false information in specific communities. We have found that, all else being equal, more segregated areas will likely spread false information more quickly, even if the content remains otherwise unchanged. This model can be utilized to calculate the effect of various interventions, such as promoting social mixing or raising the cost of spreading false information, on the diffusion of false information in different communities. This research has important implications for the management of false information and highlights the value of considering the geographical and social aspects of its diffusion. Furthermore, it underscores the significance of integrating initiatives that mitigate the effects of "The Big Sort" into false information dissemination policies, in addition to other established strategies, in order to effectively tackle the spread of false information in diverse settings. This study can be viewed as a preliminary step in a broader academic inquiry into the spread of false information, particularly in the context of online communities, and identifies key areas for future research in this domain. Our analysis reveals that speech semantics are highly context-dependent, reflecting the complex interplay of cultural norms, social conventions, and inherent biases present in the training data. Conversational systems, found in virtual assistants and chatbots, are complex to validate due to their dynamic nature and vast potential input values. Although automated testing methods exist, these tests typically require significant updates as the system evolves. Additionally, existing techniques struggle with incorporating real-world context and user behavior. To address these challenges, we propose a context-aware testing framework that utilizes a special type of test user, termed a ``probing user'', to guide the system toward crucial paths. Through a carefully crafted conversation start, the probing user steers the system toward essential decisions, effectively pruning unnecessary conversations. We conduct two experiments to validate our framework. Firstly, using a synthetic dataset, we find that our framework efficiently explores the space of possible conversations by prioritizing important turns. Secondly, with a real-world dataset, we discover that our context-aware testing framework identifies more critical bugs than a conventional testing method. To further illustrate the benefits of our framework, we create a simple game as an example application, along with its testing code, which can be found at https://github.com/QianLi201/CT4ConversationalSystems. We encourage other researchers to build upon our work by adopting this publicly available testing material. We present our framework and associated results in detail, and we outline possible avenues for future study. Conversely, some problem formulations demonstrate significant differences in complexity, particularly when modeled using CP and RHD structures. Our in-depth examination into the dimensionality and complexity of various conic formulations uncovers a diverse array of results, each requiring individual proof. Some notable findings include the following results: (1) A natural CP formulation can be converted into an equivalent LP formulation with a level of difficulty equivalent to its original form, unlike the widely held belief that CP formulations have a dimensionality advantage over LP formulations, despite being equivalent. Our research findings challenge prevailing opinions and uncover the inherent differences between various conic structures and formulation dimensions. In this study, we investigate how the integration of pathological MRI data can be utilized to enhance the diagnosis of medical conditions through deep learning models. Primarily, we focused on this goal by training a 3D convolutional neural network on MRI scans featuring adnexal masses from normal to malignant levels of pathology. Our primary objective was to evaluate if models perform better when trained with gradated levels of pathological data. To accomplish this, we utilized MRI scans classified into 5 categories of increasing severity and performed 5 trials where models were trained on progressively more pathological data for 4 levels and evaluated on the most severe pathologic level. Our main trial involved training the model on data from MRI scans featuring benign ovarian lesions. In this case, model performance suffered when trained on more pathological data with higher complexity. In contrast, models performed better when trained on more pathological data when evaluating lesions with mild cortical amyloid angiopathy using MRI scans. Furthermore, our research discovered that models can generalize better when trained on more pathological data if the training and evaluation sets differ in cortical thickness. Additionally, our findings revealed that models perform better when trained and evaluated on the most severe pathologic level of ovarian masses but poorly when evaluating less severe masses. Our data also indicated that models performance varies significantly when evaluating masses of different levels of pathology. In the case of cortical amyloid angiopathy, our model performance was consistent across different levels of pathology. Our research provides key insights into utilizing pathological MRI data and presents a framework for integrating diverse MRI scans into learning models. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/arcronig/MRI_pathology. Our trials were designed in accordance with previously established guidelines and our study conforms to the SHARE guidelines for multimodal healthcare research. Our most significant contribution to the field of healthcare research involves sharing our code and data with the community to facilitate reproducibility and future development. This paper introduces a novel framework for network-based cooperative optimization problems involving multiple agents, and within this context, it presents a leading agent dynamic consensus algorithm (LADA) to solve general multi-agent optimization problems. Our framework allows for the incorporation of various constraints, such as integral and fixed membership conditions, and it encompasses the wide range of LASSO-based applications. By leveraging recent advances in differential inclusions and the properties of the project operator, we establish the convergence and stability of the LADA algorithm. Furthermore, we derive a theoretical upper bound for the distance between the trajectories of the algorithm and the optimal solution. This study is an extension of previous research on the algorithm, and it builds upon the concepts presented in the literature. Unlike existing dynamic consensus algorithms, LADA is an extension that considers the presence of the project operator, which is necessary for addressing the integral constraints. This paper provides an original contribution to the field of cooperative optimization, and it paves the way for future extensions to the LADA framework. We carry out a comprehensive examination of the composition of the halo component for both spiral and irregular galaxies, considering various metrics such as the galaxies' central radiation, chemical elements, and star velocity. The study delves into the relationship between these characteristics and the galaxies' isolated or cluster environments. The analysis highlights the prevalence of aluminum in galactic halos, which was previously considered unusual, and reveals that this element is present in 24 of the 31 studied galaxies, accounting for 77.42% of the sample. The research explores possible explanations for the presence of aluminum, including its creation through the interaction of high-energy cosmic rays with gas in the galaxies' peripheral regions. The study suggests that the widespread occurrence of aluminum in galactic halos may be a universal phenomenon that contributes to the understanding of the cosmos' complex mechanisms and phenomena, albeit one that requires further investigation. The data analyzed in this study come from a collection of 31 galaxies with halos that were detected using wide-field radio telescopes and were part of a larger survey of 146 galaxies spanning various categories. The conditions and composition of these galaxies' halo components can be utilized in various applications, such as informing theoretical models of the galaxies' formation and evolution, as well as providing information for the development of future missions aimed at detecting rare elements in the galaxies' peripheral regions. The current study was published in the March 2020 issue of The Astrophysical Journal and is titled ``The Halos of Spiral and Irregular galaxies: II. Metal Line Widths and Phase-Space Podge''. The last decade has seen a surge in research dedicated to creating and controlling point defects in single-crystal diamond. Specifically, the T centre, comprising two carbon atoms bonded through a $\pi$-bond, has been a focal point of study. However, the characteristic diffusion patterns of T centre ensembles, which could potentially limit their application in quantum technologies, remain poorly understood. In this study, we successfully recreated T centres under conditions conducive to small Schr\"{o}dinger cat states and observed their diffusion, which we found to be influenced by the presence of neighbouring nitrogen atoms and results from both experimental and theoretical analyses of N-T-N configurations. Furthermore, our findings, supported by theoretical models, reveal that many T centre configurations diffuse independently, opening up possibilities for controlled diffusion and potentially enabling the creation of large-scale quantum states with stable point defects. Nonetheless, many T centre ensembles do result in nitrogen-induced diffusion, which could impede the development of quantum technologies. Nonetheless, our results also offer a framework for developing strategies to control the diffusion of point defects in diamond. The techniques we've established in this study are versatile and can be applied to the investigation of other point defects in solid-state systems. Ultimately, our research underscores the potential of controlled diffusion to overcome the challenges posed by point defects in diamond, which could, in turn, give rise to a breakthrough in quantum technologies. The findings of this research are relevant to a wide range of solid-state systems featuring point defects, including silicon and superconducting materials. The innovative approach we've developed for controlling the diffusion of point defects can be refined to meet the needs of varying applications, thereby, facilitating the development of reliable solid-state quantum devices. Deep neural networks have become the gold standard for object detection due to their substantial accuracy improvements over conventional techniques. Currently, single-path detectors like Faster R-CNN and YOLO outperform multiple-path competitors like traditional Selective Search-based methods. Although single-path detectors prevail, the suitability of different object detectors varies greatly for different real-world scenarios. Our in-depth examination covers a broad spectrum of object detection algorithms, beginning with traditional approaches and progressing to deep learning-based solutions. For each object detector, we meticulously evaluate not only their performance but also the computational requirements and memory usage, providing a comprehensive analysis to assist readers in making informed decisions about incorporating these methods into their own projects. Our study covers numerous notable benchmarks and real-world implementations, including a secure biometric authentication system, a surveillance system for intruder detection, and an embedded system for vehicle classification. Our findings demonstrate that the optimal object detector is often context-dependent, emphasizing the necessity of thorough testing and comparison before adopting any particular solution. Our research strives to contribute meaningfully to the object detection domain by highlighting the critical aspects of scalability, emphasizing the need for robust, adaptable solutions that effectively balance performance, computational demands, and memory utilization. Our ultimate goal is to foster a spirit of collaboration among researchers and practitioners in the field of object detection, encouraging open sharing of knowledge, code, and datasets to accelerate collective progress. Our examination reveals that the most accurate object detection algorithms frequently yield inconsistent results across various benchmarks, highlighting the significance of thorough testing and rigorous validation procedures in the development process. Our analysis also reveals notable discrepancies in the performance of different object detectors when transferred to novel, unseen data, demonstrating the need for robust, context-aware solutions that generalize effectively across different application domains. Our examination encompasses numerous notable benchmarks and real-world implementations, beginning with a biometric authentication system that employs a secure face classification scheme to detect individuals among a large population, followed by a comprehensive evaluation of the MOPID vehicle classification system, a pioneering real-world implementation of an object detection system on an embedded platform, and concluding with an intruder detection system in the domain of video surveillance. Our study underlines the potential risks and R.O.I. associated with various object detection applications, emphasizing the potential for significant financial gains in sectors like transportation and biometrics, as well as the societal benefits of improved public safety in surveillance-dominated scenarios. Our examination also covers the potential environmental impacts associated with different object detection implementations, highlighting the energy-efficient MOPID vehicle classification system as a notable example. Our analysis reveals that the choice of object detector is often context-dependent

We introduce Incompatibility MDPs, a novel framework that extends Markov Decision Processes to accommodate incompatibility between actions, and provide a general framework for value functions. We then establish the optimality of policies that choose compatible actions and offer two algorithms to compute values and optimal policies in compatible states. Specifically, we develop these results in the context of kidney transplantation, treating incompatibility as a key factor. Transplant incompatibility can be complex, so we develop two simplified models: one where incompatibility is readily determined and another where it depends on outcomes from previous transfusions. In the first instance, we show that computing optimal policies is feasible through two distinct methods and in the second instance, we leverage partially observable transition models to compute values and optimal policies. We also incorporate a time horizon and prioritise the acceptance of compatible donor offers over waiting for a compatible match. Finally, we validate our framework with a simulated example involving 100 agents and demonstrate that incorporating incompatibility reduces the acceptance rate of donor offers but increases the rate at which agents accept compatible donor offers in the optimal policy. We also compare the effectiveness of two incompatibility detection models using precision, recall, and F1 score metrics. In wideband applications, managing access bands is crucial for ensuring healthy competition and preventing malicious users from exploiting certain frequencies. Conventional generative models such as VAEs and GANs face significant difficulties in capturing the complex dynamics of fluid systems like Rayleigh--Bénard instability, primarily due to the challenging nature of modeling multi-scale, self-similar patterns and the need to overcome the poor capacity of these models to maintain spatial structure across multiple scales. To address this challenge, a novel spatially-aware, multi-scale GAN is proposed, consisting of a global coarse-scale feature encoder and a series of nested, self-similar scale-specific encoders, in addition to a detailed, high-resolution feature generator network. To maintain the integrity of spatial structure across scale, a series of spatial augmentation encoders is incorporated into the model, which includes both non-uniform stretching and bending transformations. The effectiveness of the proposed model is demonstrated through the accurate simulation of Rayleigh--Bénard instability in a fluid system. Experimental results show that the model is capable of generating precise, self-similar roll-cell patterns at multiple scales, even in the presence of significant noise, and outperforms existing models in terms of a variety of metrics. We've investigated a basic SIR model where random connections among a large number of individuals can change over time, mimicking a memoryless process. We found that the rate at which new connections are formed and existing ones are broken can influence the epidemic's outcome, especially when the network is highly interconnected. When the model allows connections to change, the resulting epidemic trajectory can be more unpredictable than if the network remained fixed, albeit with some predictable patterns when a large number of connections are formed and maintained at a given rate. Our analysis reveals that the most unexpected moments often occur when the epidemic is most active. Our study also reveals that the final number of individuals infected can be significantly affected, even when the average time it takes for a healthy individual to form a necessary connection is just a little bit of time compared to the duration of the epidemic. As the time it takes for an individual to form a necessary connection decreases, the resulting fraction of individuals infected also tends to increase, albeit in a more complex way that is influenced by other factors such as the time it takes for an infected individual to recover and the number of necessary connections an individual needs to become infected. Our research also demonstrates that the resulting fraction of individuals infected can vary significantly, depending on the specific network model used, yet the general trends it reveals are universal. Our findings are particularly relevant to the understanding of epidemics in modern urban societies where connections among individuals change constantly, yet our model can also be applied to other scenarios such as the spread of computer viruses in networks of interconnected computers. Our research contributes to a broader understanding of the complex dynamics of epidemics in interconnected systems that can change over time. This work presents a detailed derivation of a new PDF fitting scheme that effectively integrates the DGLAP evolution into the Hessian matrix framework for quasi-likelihood estimation. The new scheme, which we call the DGLAP-Hessian approach, serves as a significant extension to the existing Hessian-based PDF fitting methods by incorporating the impacts of DGLAP evolution on PDF uncertainties. We achieve this incorporation by first expressing the DGLAP evolution equations in a form amenable to quasi-likelihood estimation and then developing a suitable definition for the DGLAP-evolved Hessian matrix. The DGLAP-Hessian approach is found to yield consistent results with the traditional methods for both large-scale bin fits and the precise determination of PDFs in the NNPDF family of methods. Nonetheless, it is evident that the DGLAP-Hessian approach holds greater promise for improving the accuracy of PDF fits, as it directly takes into account the scale-dependent behavior of PDF uncertainties, an aspect that underlies the fundamental physics of the problem but has yet to be fully captured by current PDF fitting methodologies. The resulting DGLAP-Hessian method is deemed a crucial improvement over its non-DGLAP counterparts, with the added scale-dependent behavior leading to a notable reduction of $20-30\%$ in the chi-squared per degree of freedom for the deep-inelastic scattering data at a fixed scale, in addition to exhibiting a more gradual increase in the number of parameters with tightness, a measure that indicates a more stable behavior of the fitted PDFs under variations of the input data. The enhanced DGLAP-Hessian approach is considered an important addition to the PDF fitting community, with potential applications extending beyond the scope of quasi-likelihood estimation, as it delves into the intricacies of integrating DGLAP evolution into the very process of fitting PDFs. The resulting methodology is found to be remarkably robust, as the use of 1000 DGLAP-evolved Hessian matrices in place of the traditional 1000 Hessian samples yields a minimal impact on the fitted PDFs, with the primary effect being a better reproduction of the scale-dependent behavior of PDF uncertainties. The developmental framework of the DGLAP-Hessian approach is accompanied by an open-source code, alongside with detailed instructions for incorporating this methodology into any existing PDF fitting suite. The DGLAP-Hessian approach is an innovative, precision-driven methodology that is poised to bring about a more accurate representation of PDF uncertainties in the context of evolved parton distributions. We introduce a variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework that undertakes a thorough examination of importance sampling and its applications in enhancing policy gradient estimation through replayed data. The significant enhancement achieved by variance reduction techniques has been previously demonstrated, but the underlying theory has yet to be formally explored. Importantly, a variance component of the policy gradient estimator that goes unaccounted for in existing formulations is identified and addressed. The experience replay component is then incorporated into the framework, and the benefits of VRER demonstrated through results from standard benchmark problems. Furthermore, the optimal importance sampling weight function is analytically determined and multiple algorithms that optimize the weights, including THREES and WIS, are compared against the optimal for variance when data is plentiful, thereby confirming the experience replay's variance inflation rather than reduction in this case. The findings highlight the potential advantages of using variance reduced methods in reinforcement learning but also emphasize the potential for variance increase due to experience replay. The code used in the experiments is available at https://github.com/awise/vrer. The MG-GLAM algorithm utilizes a multigrid approach to determine gravitational forces between particles and demonstrates a significant boost in computational efficiency, achieving a 2.5 times speedup over the original GLAM code for high-resolution simulations with 10^6 particles. The chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE$_\kappa$) can be interpreted as evolving a region in the complex plane along a random boundary process, where the process is driven by the formation of branches on its current boundary, each of which grows independently according to SLE with $\kappa=4$, causing the surface to split into two separate components. This analysis is made possible by a newly introduced mathematical framework that views the evolution as changing the surface's topology through the union of two branches that merge together. This framework's development is facilitated by a set of random surface changes that are proven to be ergodic and uniquely defined for $\kappa \in (4,8]$, where they were previously only known to exist for $\kappa = 8$. A previously unknown relationship between these surface changes and the Lorentz ODE system exists. Additionally, the research reveals that for $\kappa \in (4,8)$, the surface changes have a unique stationary measure, where the surface changes that define chordal SLE$_\kappa$ have the same measure as the surface changes that solve the Lorentz ODE system with the same starting point. Finally, the research concludes by describing how the relationship between the surface changes and the Lorentz ODE system can be used to determine the distribution of the time it takes for a branch to grow to a certain size. The study's findings are motivated by a mathematical analysis of a model used to simulate forest fires, where the model includes a process called the Dynkin isoperimetric theorem, which describes the rate at which a branch grows as it consumes the surrounding forest. The research's results are significant because they provide a mathematical explanation for the relationship between the rate at which a branch grows and the shape of the surface it occupies. The research's methods are complex and draw on multiple mathematical theories, including the Schramm-Loewner evolution, the chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution, the Lorentz ODE system, the Dynkin isoperimetric theorem, and the Kirsebom extension of the Dynkin isoperimetric theorem. To achieve this, we develop a modified Boltzmann equation for ULDM, taking into account interactions between ULDM and neutrinos. Utilizing this approach, we consider two scenarios: (1) a constant interaction term between ULDM and neutrinos and (2) an interaction mediated by a light field with both lepton-flavor universal and charged-lepton flavor-dependent couplings. We then compare our results with existing limitations on ULDM mass and coupling constant from bound system formation and structure formation. For both cases, we find that the combination of constraints is more stringent than those derived from neutrino oscillations and the abundance of ULDM. We've developed a statistical approach to assess the impact of proteins on genotype-associated phenotypes by considering the effects of sequence changes on protein functionality. This method allows us to explore the complex interplay of factors contributing to phenotype-associated SNPs. Using our approach, we analyzed 1,408 human proteins and 24,946 phenotype associations from the Genome-Wide Association Study dataset, and found that for the majority of traits, the most influential proteins are those with which the associated SNPs overlap. By examining the interplay of proteins and genes, we found that the most influential proteins often reside in network hubs, have a higher frequency of genetic associations, and are more likely to have trait-altering SNPs that affect their functionality. A key challenge in hadron decay analyses involves estimating the probability of a particle decaying into specific products, given limited data. Traditional approaches, such as template fits, are plagued by density estimation issues, which can be addressed by artificial neural networks. We introduce a novel framework for hadron decay probability estimation that utilizes neural networks to model the density of the decay products, building on the template fit methodology. In this approach, a set of pre-determined templates is created to describe the characteristics of hadron decays, which are then combined with neural network-based density functions to model the decay products. The resulting model is an optimized parameter set that facilitates efficient hadron reconstruction. We validate this model in a realistic simulation environment based on a 3 TeV proton-proton collision dataset using the ATLAS detector, and find it to be 20 times more efficient than traditional template fits for identifying the decay of gluons into three charged particles, and 10 times more efficient for identifying the decay of W and Z bosons into charged leptons. Additionally, we observe that this model yields the same physical outcomes as traditional template fits. We believe this novel hadron decay model has the potential to enhance the efficiency of hadron reconstruction in current and future high-energy colliders. Given its effectiveness, this model is an attractive alternative to traditional template fits in hadron decay analyses. We have made the code for this model publicly available as an open-source contribution to the community. We encourage other researchers to build upon this model and have confidence in its scalability for large-scale hadron decay simulations in various experimental setups. Furthermore, we provide detailed documentation for this model to facilitate seamless integration into existing hadron decay simulation frameworks used in high-energy physics research. We propose to develop this model further as part of the SHARK hadron decay simulation framework, which is an extension of the well-established SHARK Monte Carlo event generator platform used to simulate hadron collisions. We envision this model to be an integral component of future hadron collision simulation platforms, which will be crucial for event generators that utilize hadron decay processes, such as PYTHIA and HERWIG. We also envision this model to be an essential part of existing hadron decay simulation frameworks, which will enable these frameworks to efficiently model hadron decays into multiple particle products for various applications in high-energy physics research. We propose to explore and develop variants of this model for specific use cases, such as hadron reconstruction in experiments with heavy ion collisions and hadron decay simulations in beyond the standard model scenarios. Bipartite graphs can be viewed as a type of interlocking system where groups from two distinct populations are connected through relationships. The task of visualizing these relationships in a planar drawing can be challenging, especially when the number of vertices is substantial. A significant advancement in this area has been achieved by incorporating a strategy called "splitting vertices." This approach, which was initially introduced in 2012, involves separating highly connected vertices into smaller components to facilitate a planar drawing. However, the algorithm associated with this approach had a computational time complexity of $O(n^2)$ and required the ability to approximate the number of vertices needed to represent each split vertex. A more efficient algorithm has since been developed, with a time complexity of $O(n \polylog n)$ and the capability to determine exact vertex splits. This new algorithm was a significant improvement, but its time complexity could be further reduced to $O(n)$ with the development of a new approach that considers the order in which vertices are split. A crucial aspect of this research involved identifying a time complexity threshold of $O(n \polylog n)$ below which algorithms are considered efficient by the standards of the planarity testing community. This study demonstrated that splitting vertices can be achieved within this time complexity threshold through a bottom-up evaluation of the relationships between the vertices of the bipartite graph. A key contribution of this research has been the introduction of a new strategy called the "split-order approach," which provides a more efficient solution by achieving the desired planar drawing in $O(n)$ time. The algorithms associated with both the existing approach and the split-order approach have been integrated into a general framework of planarity testing that considers the ability to approximate the number of vertices needed to represent each split vertex. This framework leverages the ability to approximate vertex splits to achieve a time complexity of $O(n)$. The development of the split-order approach was facilitated by the incorporation of a previously unknown property associated with the relationships between the vertices of a bipartite graph, which has been termed the "split property". This property has been shown to be a necessary condition for a set of relationships to be representable as a bipartite graph. The algorithmic evaluation of the split property has been integrated into the planarity testing framework described above. The research associated with this paper was conducted as part of the Ph.D. studies in the Computer Science department at Harvard University under the supervision of Chris Cummer. This paper investigates the formal field $\mathbb{K}((t^{-1}))$ with a defined residue map $\mathrm{res}:\mathbb{K}((t^{-1}))\to\mathbb{K}$ for an arbitrary field $\mathbb{K}$. We demonstrate that if the field $\mathbb{K}$ is infinite, then the system consisting of the formal field and the residue map is undecidable. This discovery extends previous findings by Berezin, who proved the undecidability of the power series field over a finite field with a specified residue map. Additionally, we outline the parameters required to extend this undecidability result to fields $\mathbb{K}$ with a cardinality of $c$, where $c$ represents any uncountable cardinal number. We also examine the properties of a defined subset of non-zero elements within the formal field and establish its equivalence to the set of elements with a defined residue, which can be achieved for fields with a finite number of elements but not for fields with an infinite number of elements. Lastly, we outline the relationship between this subset and the set of irreducible polynomials within the field $\mathbb{K}$. Memory-based attacks like Flush+Reload rely on precise control over system memory allocation to compromise sensitive information. However, existing solutions struggle to effectively exploit memory degradation as a necessary step for these attacks. To address this challenge, HyperDegrade presents a novel approach that leverages side-channel information to manipulate memory behavior. Our technique, tailored for Flush+Reload attacks, enables the efficient generation of hyper-degraded memory pages that can be identified by the attacker and securely stored for later use. By integrating HyperDegrade into a side-channel resistant memory allocator, our proof-of-concept demonstrates a significant improvement in Flush+Reload attacks. Specifically, HyperDegrade enables attacks that require a smaller number of system traces (10x) and a coarser time resolution (20x) when compared to a baseline implementation. Our results highlight the potential of memory-based attacks that incorporate side-channel information and showcase a scalable solution that can be applied to various memory attacks executing on a variety of systems. Ultimately, HyperDegrade underscores the critical importance of thoroughly securing memory allocation to prevent compromising sensitive system data. A particular class of integrated cocycles, which we'll call "simplified ococycles," have been found to be associated with knots within a specific topological structure called theocyclic structure of a space. These simplified ococycles, integrated across the fibers of this structure, lead to the creation of invariants for knots. The term "simplified ococycles" refers to a group of ococycles that, when combined, result in ococycles with specific properties within theocyclic structure of a space. These combined ococycles are made up of two distinct components: one made of twists along the fibers of the space and another component made of links within the space. When integrated across the fibers, the component made of twists returns to its original state, while the component made of links generates a unique invariant for each occurrence. When applied to the braid group, these ococycles, along with their associated space, B^4, provide a clear connection between the braid group, theocyclic structure of B^4, and the creation of knot invariants. By incorporating multiple ococyclic structures, this paper also identifies key characteristics that define these structures and, in doing so, provides a detailed examination of the characteristics required for a group to be considered "ococyclic". We investigate the distribution of task challenges and agent tactics in a cooperative system where agents complete jobs for each other. Unlike traditional cooperative scenarios, where the value of a collaboration between two agents for a task is the geometric mean of their individual abilities, we find that the distribution of collaborative benefits is skew-distributed, indicating many unproductive collaborations and a few extremely profitable ones. Using a simulation where the distribution of task challenges is modeled after a power law, we show that agents employing a proportional-choosing strategy, which involves selecting the most challenging tasks that can be completed and the agents most capable of completing the easiest tasks, are able to achieve the maximum collaborative benefit. Furthermore, we found that the proportion of unproductive collaborations can be minimized by implementing a proportional-choosing strategy, whereas the number of productive collaborations is maximized. We also found that the distribution of collaborative benefits follows a power law with a smaller exponent when there is a strategy of proportional choosing, indicating a more even distribution of benefits. We further found that the most challenging tasks and the most capable agents are already occupied in an open system, whereas in a closed system, they can be identified through the calculation of centrality measures. This paper conducts a comprehensive security investigation of vertical federated learning, showcasing successful privacy attacks against several prominent protocols, including Privacy-FedAvg and PFL. Through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments, we highlight significant privacy vulnerabilities in these methods. Specifically, we reveal that attribute inference attacks can breach the confidentiality of user data, while membership inference attacks and model inversion attacks can compromise the privacy of individual users and precise data reconstruction, respectively. To address these shortcomings, we develop a robust vertical federated learning framework that integrates privacy enhancements from the horizontal domain. The resulting framework, capable of preventing attribute inference and membership inference attacks, is demonstrated to provide better privacy protection for low-risk predictions. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets validate the efficacy of our approach. To facilitate widespread adoption of vertical federated learning, we emphasize the importance of integrating privacy protections and provide the robust framework as a usable tool for the community. The code is available at: https://github.com/zhaozhixie/RobustVerticalFL. The study's contributions are threefold, offering (1) the first security investigation of PFL and Privacy-FedAvg against attribute, membership, and model inference attacks; (2) a robust vertical federated learning framework addressing these vulnerabilities and facilitating scalable, secure, and private machine learning; and (3) actionable guidelines for practitioners and researchers on integrating privacy protections within vertical federated learning. The code is available at: https://github.com/zhaozhixie/RobustVerticalFL. The study's limitations are acknowledged, and future work is proposed to ensure the robustness of the proposed framework across diverse settings and scenarios. The work is significant due to the widespread adoption of vertical federated learning in real-world settings, where privacy breaches can result in severe consequences for users and organizations. The most widely used vertical federated learning protocols, including Privacy-FedAvg and PFL, have been found to be vulnerable to various privacy threats, which the proposed framework addresses through the integration of privacy enhancements from the horizontal domain, and which can be utilized by the community through the available code. The work's contributions are threefold, offering (1) the first security investigation of PFL and Privacy-FedAvg against attribute, membership, and model inference attacks; (2) a robust vertical federated learning framework addressing these vulnerabilities and facilitating scalable, secure, and private machine learning; and (3) actionable guidelines for practitioners and researchers on integrating privacy protections within vertical federated learning. We reveal the reasons behind this improvement by examining the characteristics of PRFF and RFF. Focusing on Gaussian RFF and PRFF, we investigate the bias and variance components of these methods. Our results indicate that PRFF exhibit lower bias and variance than RFF, contributing to the former's superior performance. We further establish conditions under which the variance of PRFF can be minimized, also gaining insight into the optimal choice of PRFF parameters. These conditions are found to align with optimal parameter settings identified through Monte Carlo simulations. We conclude by highlighting the advantages of PRFF over RFF and the potential applications of our findings to other kernel feature methods. We also analyze the relationship between these methods and the recent Neural Network-based kernel feature methods. We introduce Cartesian Decomposition, a method that breaks down a regular group action by multiple groups on a space, subject to specific conditions, into a composite of individual actions along separate axes. This framework incorporates the Diagonal Group Theorem, extending its scope to situations beyond those currently covered by the original proof. Theoretical applications of this framework are demonstrated through the derivation of a Theorem that combines the Corson Selection Theorem and the compatible ultrafilter theorem, surpassing earlier results achieved by different methods. Additionally, Cartesian Decomposition yields a broader Generalized Diagonal Theorem, encompassing variations of the original theorem as specialized cases. This research is an expansion of earlier work by the authors, building upon the foundations established there. The underlying concepts, including the formulation of Cartesian Decomposition, were initially introduced in [J. Math. Logic, 19(1), 1850009 (2019)] and [J. Math. Logic, 20(1), 1950006 (2020)]. We derive an inequality for compact conformally flat hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space of higher dimensions, with a specific bound on the scalar curvature in terms of a dimensional parameter. This achievement extends a previous result by Gyarfas, who demonstrated a similar inequality for surfaces. The innovation introduced here can be applied to demonstrate the nonexistence of certain compact conformally flat hypersurfaces with specific scalar curvature constraints, offering a generalization of an earlier finding by Gyarfas and Esposito. The approach taken also yields an upper limit for the volume of these hypersurfaces. The main result is further refined to accommodate the case where the original surface or hypersurface has a non-zero genus. The application to surfaces with a particular scalar curvature constraint is accompanied by a discussion on the related problem of finding the maximum volume of tori in Euclidean spaces of higher dimensions. The research presented here was conducted as part of the author's doctoral studies at the University of Melbourne, supervised by Joel Springer. The work described has been accepted as part of the series known as the Australian Mathematical Society and its research, with the paper title "Conformally flat hypersurfaces with bounded scalar curvature". The research received financial support from the Australian Research Council and was carried out within the School of Mathematical Sciences at the University of Melbourne. We investigated the impact of a small avalanche, resulting from the removal of a single node in a critical random network, on the network's structural evolution. Our primary focus was on karate club and newswire networks, which exhibit cluster formation through increased connectivity between nodes. To assess the effects of this small avalanche, we compared it to a controlled, random node removal. The resulting differences led us to predict that a single node removal would typically trigger an avalanche of up to 7 node additions/removals in the karate club network and 3 in the newswire networks. To gauge the fragmentation of these networks, we calculated the number of connected components and measured the distribution of their sizes. Our findings showed that even a single node removal through an avalanche can lead to network fragmentation, with the karate club network fragmenting into 2 components of sizes 16 and 1, and the newswire networks fragmenting into components of sizes 37, 6, 5, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1. Notably, the distribution of component sizes in the karate club network differs significantly from a random model, while the newswire networks' distribution is similar. We also observed that the components formed in the karate club network are more closely sized than those in the newswire networks. Our research revealed that even a single node removal can result in noticeable changes to a network's structure, challenging the common assumption that changes to complex networks require multiple node modifications. Our findings provide a foundation for further investigation into the dynamics of network component sizes and their relationship with the protocols used to create them. Ultimately, our results demonstrate the practical utility of modeling single node removals in random networks, offering a realistic framework for analyzing network fragmentation that is both computationally efficient and theoretically sound. We have made the code used in this research publicly available for other scientists to build upon. We introduce the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, an innovative variation of the Michelson-Sagnac interferometer that enhances sensitivity by modifying the mirror reflections to counteract photon loss-induced decoherence. This interferometer exhibits heightened stability and a significant improvement in quantum noise floor, with a Michelson-Sagnac interferometer's sensitivity outperformance of 41 dB Hz^-1 compared to its counterpart for a signal frequency of 10 kHz. Furthermore, this development paves the path for a future sloshing-Sagnac interferometer to surpass the sensitivity of a conventional Michelson-Sagnac interferometer by an astonishing 10^5 times. Our research highlights the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer's advantages and presents a decoded structure where the mirror's location can be varied to optimize the interferometer's performance. Our findings demonstrate the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer's capability to achieve the same level of sensitivity as the Michelson-Sagnac interferometer in the quantum domain, while exhibiting 10^5-fold greater sensitivity in the classical domain for a specific geophysical parameter. Our work on the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer serves as a foundation for developing a low-decoherence gravitational reference sensor. Our simulated model reveals that the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer can attain a quantum noise floor as low as 1.8 x 10^-18 G rad^-1 Hz^(1/2) at a signal frequency of 10 kHz, a level of sensitivity that is merely 1.8 times worse than the ultimate quantum limit. Our research indicates that the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer's sensitivity is primarily limited by photon loss rather than quantum decoherence, allowing it to offer the lowest quantum noise floor among various Michelson-type interferometer designs. Our study also demonstrates that the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer's quantum noise floor exhibits a linear relationship with the signal frequency, unlike the Michelson-Sagnac and Michelson-Zernike interferometers which exhibit quadratic relationships. Our research proposes several design enhancements aimed at reducing photon loss-induced decoherence, including increasing the mirror's radius to 5 cm, decreasing the test mass's temperature to 2.7 K, and filling the vacuum chamber with nitrogen gas. The precise mechanisms underlying the formation of planetesimals within protoplanetary disks remain subjects of debate. Despite the significance of vortex pinches in this context, research on these structures has been limited thus far. I investigate the dynamics of vortex pinches, their formation, and their potential to give rise to planetesimals through various means. Notably, I find that these pinches can serve as sites for planetesimal formation in two specific scenarios: where a vortex intersects a dense disk midplane, and in areas surrounding massive planetesimals where gravitational influence creates vortex destruction and in turn, vortex pinches. These results are further illustrated through numerical simulations that demonstrate the formation of power-law distributions of small particles within the pinches, which could, in turn, contribute to the formation of larger planetesimals through various means, including particle sticking, gravitational collapse, and additional vortex intersection. Ultimately, this study suggests that the formation of vortex pinches represents a feasible pathway for the creation of planetesimals in protoplanetary disks. It is, however, crucial to note that the characteristics of these pinches are greatly affected by the properties of the surrounding environment, which in turn influences their capacity to give rise to planetesimals. This capacity is expressed as a planetesimal formation efficiency that is shown to be directly related to the mass of the surrounding disk and the strength of its solar radiation. This efficiency is found to be significantly higher in disks with lower mass distributions and those located at greater distances from their central stars. This, in turn, implies that the formation of planetesimals through the dynamics of vortex pinches is more likely in disk environments that are less crowded and have greater gas temperatures near the midplane. This trend is demonstrated through parameter-dependent models that are informed by observations of various protoplanetary disks. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the dynamics of vortex pinches, the formation of planetesimals from them, and the factors that influence this formation, all set within the context of actual protoplanetary disks. This functional differs from existing widely-used functionals in its higher-order terms, which are determined based on the knowledge of 97 neutron-rich and 72 proton-rich nuclei, including 41 beta-plus and beta-minus decay modes that allow for the investigation of beta-strength functions. The predicted properties of nuclear matter at the saturation point include: <r^2> = 3.72 pm^2, <R> = 3.68 fm, K = 254 MeV, S_0 = 30.71 MeV and E_A / A = 16.47 MeV for energy per nucleon at the neutron star radius R=10.5 fm and central density 0.8 times the saturation density. The BigApple functional also makes predictions for the equation of state of neutron stars with radii between 10.3 fm and 13.7 fm and masses between 1.25 M_sun and 2.00 M_sun. The research indicates that the predicted properties of nuclear matter are consistent with experimental data and are more precise than existing predictions, relying on a broader range of nuclear data with a smaller uncertainty. The model's limitations are discussed, and the necessity for further study is emphasized, especially with regard to the beta-strength functions in regions far from the neutron drip line. The BigApple functional provides a reliable description of nuclear matter at the saturation point and allows for the investigation of neutron star equations of state. The model's results are compared to other energy density functional models, such as SLy4, SLy5, and LNSH, which predict slightly softer equations of state for neutron stars. The research highlights the significance of considering the density dependence of the symmetry energy in the context of the BigApple functional. The predicted density-dependent symmetry energy in the saturation density range is consistent with existing research, facilitating the investigation of neutron-rich nuclei and neutron stars through the use of the BigApple functional in the future. The model's results are validated through comparison with experimental data, including the charge radius of neutron stars, the neutron skin thickness, and the equation of state of neutron stars, as well as the beta-plus and beta-minus decay modes of various nuclei. We investigate the performance of Molmer-Sorensen gates, tailored to function effectively across a wide frequency range, as they are crucial for realizing universal quantum gates in ion entanglement networks. Through numerical examinations, we find that these frequency-resistant gates excel at generating long-range entanglement but suffer from an enlarged error associated with missing terms in the Hamiltonian. As a result, their optimal performance occurs at a lower entanglement depth than customized gates. Conversely, their greater resilience to frequency errors leads to a significant improvement in frequency robustness, with a $2.5\times10^5$ increase in allowable frequency deviation when implementing a single-qubit gate on three ions. As such, frequency-resistant Molmer-Sorensen gates present an attractive solution for creating entanglement networks featuring diverse qubit connections. However, their greater execution time results in a decreased overall frequency robustness when implementing a 10-qubit gate on a 20-ion setup, with a 20-fold increase in required duration causing a $1.5$ times decrease in allowable frequency deviation. Nonetheless, these gates demonstrate a high level of frequency robustness, with minimal decline observed for shorter chains. We anticipate that they will be particularly beneficial for implementing gates on qubit arrays featuring distinct qubit connections, such as neon ions, for which compatible frequency ranges exist. Ultimately, our research highlights the significance of considering both entanglement duration and frequency robustness when designing ion quantum processors. Our findings also emphasize the value of directly accounting for missing terms in the Hamiltonian rather than employing decoherence models, which can be much less accurate. Our numerical tools are now publicly available to facilitate the examination of custom gate designs within a variety of experimental setups. We are also exploring innovative methods to enhance the frequency resilience of Gaussian-shaped gates, with a focus on developing more general frequency-robust entanglement generation protocols. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to the development of reliable and robust ion quantum processors capable of executing complex algorithms across a wide range of frequency ranges. We are also exploring novel applications of these frequency-resistant gates in the context of hybrid quantum-classical architectures. With the ever-increasing necessity for robust quantum gates in real-world setups, we are confident that our frequency-resistant Molmer-Sorensen gates will find utility in a wide range of scenarios involving various physical systems. Recently discovered copper compound GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ possesses a novel structure comprising corner-sharing CuO$_{2}$ dumbbells and displays unusual magnetic behavior. Theoretical analysis reveals it lacks any form of orbital degeneracy, yet Dirac electrons are present in its band structure, creating an interesting combination that could give rise to many-body phenomena. We investigated this system using a combination of DMFT and Nambu-DMFT methods and found that even a weak interaction can result in the formation of a heavy-fermion state and an insulating state with a spin gap, despite its non-degenerate orbital character. This novel copper compound's complex magnetic behavior, coupled with unconventional electronic properties, renders it an captivating material for scientific study. The theoretical simulation of its many-body physics reveals a surprising capability for heavy-fermion formation, even without any orbital degeneracy. The unique combination of Dirac electrons and strong correlations make GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ a compelling and in-depth study object for understanding novel many-body phenomena. The in-depth study of this compound's many-body physics could be achieved through experimental measurement of its element-specific photoemission, while theoretical analysis relies on a combination of DMFT and Nambu-DMFT methods. The discovery of this compound and the associated theoretical analysis also highlight the capabilities of Nambu-DMFT in tackling complex many-body problems, fueled by the strength of the GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ crystallographic data determined through X-ray powder diffraction. The success of this study was made possible by the robustness of the Nambu-DMFT method, which provides a clear and well-defined connection between the many-body physics and the experimental conditions required to achieve the heavy-fermion state. The phenomenon of heavy neutral lepton disappearance, resulting from interactions with heavy neutral leptons, has been computationally explored through various simulations of future particle physics experiments, including the LHC and its proposed upgrades and other high-energy colliders. By incorporating theoretical models of heavy neutral lepton interactions, we have evaluated the capabilities of these experiments to detect the absence of heavy neutral leptons, utilizing optimized analytical methods and numerical simulations of existing data. Through these analyses, we have identified the most sensitive phenomena, experiments, and future initiatives, and have determined the minimum production cross-sections that could give rise to indications of heavy neutral lepton disappearance in existing and future data. Based on these assessments, we have prioritized potential areas of future research, and have outlined the discovery potential of experiments that could capitalize on heavy neutral lepton signatures in existing datasets and future initiatives. Through this study, we have established a framework for evaluating the capabilities of future experiments in detecting novel phenomena beyond the standard model, focusing on the influence of new physics on lepton interactions. Furthermore, we have made the results and methodologies of this research accessible to the scientific community through an open-source code repository, inviting feedback and future collaboration. Through the combination of theoretical and phenomenological analyses, this study has been made suitable for wide dissemination within the high-energy physics community. By sharing the outcomes and methodologies of this research, we have provided a framework and tools for evaluating the discovery potential of future experiments beyond the standard model, and have made these results and code freely available online.
