This paper explores the potential of language models that combine $n$-gram networks and neural models to enhance their capabilities in various language-related tasks including machine translation, summarization, and text generation. Our analysis reveals that merged models consistently surpass the performance of their individual components across these tasks, as demonstrated by results showing a 1.5% increase in translation accuracy from a 5-gram HMM model when combined with a neural translation model, and a 2.5% improvement in summarization F-score when combining a neural model with a 4-gram based maximum entropy model. Our findings also reveal that the optimal weight for combining the models varies significantly across different tasks and data sets, necessitating the need for a data-driven approach to determine the optimal weighting, and that the benefits of combined models are most pronounced when the underlying models have significantly different capabilities. Our proposed algorithm utilizes a data-driven approach to calculate the optimal weight for combining the models, and provides a general framework for integrating $n$-gram and neural models that can be tailored to accommodate diverse language tasks and underlying model architectures. Our experiments across three tasks and six datasets reveal that our proposed algorithm is a superior alternative to conventional maximum likelihood estimation. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at the URL https://github.com/ouraiSensei/nngram-mix. Our proposed algorithm is a versatile integration framework that can be applied to a wide range of language tasks and underlying model architectures, and provides a valuable resource for the community to build upon. Our experiments demonstrate that the combination of $n$-gram and neural models can be a valuable asset in developing practical NLP systems that balance performance with the resources required. Our findings highlight the potential of merged models to support the development of NLP applications in resource-constrained settings, and our proposed algorithm and associated code enable other researchers to explore this exciting possibility with the ease of simply modifying the existing code. Our research showcases the versatility of merged models, and our results encourage other researchers to experiment with combining different types of models that have been developed to tackle the challenges of NLP. 3D face reconstruction is a well-known issue that involves constructing a 3D face model from two-dimensional images when the view is unknown. In order to tackle this challenge, researchers often use pose-dependent and pose-independent models to represent a face. These models are typically trained using single-view 3D face reconstructions, which are considered less than ideal due to being biased and suboptimal for handling varying view factors. In response to these limitations, a new model called Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet) has been developed to model a 3D face as both a set of latent factors and a face mesh. Unlike conventional approaches, SADRNet is capable of reconstructing a face from varying view factors without the need for additional training data. In order to accommodate changing view factors, the model incorporates a mechanism called a 'look-up' module that aligns the face mesh with a self-aligned facial structure in real-time. In order to facilitate the modeling process, a new face code space was developed that considers both pose-dependent and pose-independent factors. In order to validate the model's effectiveness, a challenging multi-view 3D face reconstruction task was created that involves reconstructing a 3D face from varying view factors using a single image. In order to execute this reconstruction, a large dataset called the CelebF was developed that comprises over 210,000 high-quality images of faces from over 52,000 unique individuals. In order to further challenge the model, the reconstruction task was configured to reconstruct a 3D face from an arbitrary view factor between 0 to 60 degrees with the model being evaluated based on the reconstructed 3D face when the view factor is known in advance. In order to accommodate this scenario, a new dataset called the CelebF60 was developed that comprises over 140,000 3D face reconstructions from varying view factors between 0 to 60 degrees with the corresponding face codes. Precise database testing is crucial, and its difficulty escalates with growing databases. Our proposed approach tackles this challenge by introducing a novel, accurate method for completing missing entry values during execution. Unlike existing strategies that rely on approximate techniques, our framework guarantees exact results, even when certain entry values are unknown. Our technique leverages the underlying structure of SQL commands and employs a two-step process to fill in missing values. Firstly, it identifies commands whose missing values can be determined with certainty and secondly, it determines the values for the remaining commands with missing entries. Our algorithm achieves this by using a set of rules that take into account the relationships between tables and the availability of entries. We have thoroughly tested our approach on extensive datasets and benchmark results demonstrate its superior performance, surpassing even the ideal case achieved through complete database testing. Additionally, our technique has a linear time complexity and a constant factor of two in relation to the size of the database. Our approach also yields a precise solution for the problem of complete database testing, surpassing the existing best-known approximation algorithms in both efficiency and accuracy. Our research further extends existing theory regarding the worst-case and expected time complexities of testing precise databases. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed approach provides significant improvements over existing approximate strategies, achieving a 90% success rate in the most challenging scenarios, whereas the current state-of-the-art strategy struggles to achieve a 30% success rate in such cases. Our research has far-reaching implications for Precise Database Testing, testing of combined systems, and testing of probabilistic systems. Our proposed framework receives positive feedback from an industry partner from a major technology firm, highlighting its potential practical value. This improvement aims to provide more accurate and stable estimates of model stability and accuracy. Theoretical analysis indicates that J-K-fold cross validation yields superior performance metrics compared to K-fold cross validation, with specific numerical examples demonstrating its benefits. A computational study involving real-world datasets shows that J-K-fold cross validation outperforms standard K-fold cross validation in terms of both model accuracy and stability. This work's contributions are twofold, as it not only advances the K-fold cross validation methodology but also provides current benchmark results for machine learning algorithms to strive towards. A relevant observation is that the most suitable J and K values vary depending on the underlying problem and available data. A significant challenge in designing efficient artificial neural networks is creating a reliable training process that produces accurate and representative training data. We introduce the Teacher-Student Architecture, a versatile framework consisting of a lightweight student network and a high-performance teacher network, which generates informative training data to guide the student through repeated iterations. We demonstrated the benefits of this framework in relation to existing methods, with the student network achieving a 2.5 times reduction in parameters and a 3 times decrease in operations, while maintaining performance comparable to that of the teacher network in classification tasks. Additionally, we applied this architecture to enhance the efficiency of SqueezeNet, AlexNet, and VGGNet, achieving notable improvements over the original networks in tasks like image classification, facial recognition, and object detection. Our framework has the added benefit of allowing the creation of more accurate lightweight networks, with the SqueezeNet student network, for example, achieving a 1.5 times boost in classification accuracy while maintaining the same level of complexity. We open-sourced our code and models to facilitate the widespread adoption of efficient artificial neural networks. We also contribute a benchmark for evaluating the efficiency of artificial neural networks, highlighting the advantages of Teacher-Student Architectures in achieving a perfect balance between performance and efficiency. We anticipate that this framework will serve as a viable option for industries requiring the deployment of artificial neural networks on devices with limited resources. We have made our code and models publicly available at https://github.com/HengtaiCao/TSA. We have also established a benchmark for evaluating the efficiency of artificial neural networks, which we invite other researchers to build upon and contribute to, available at https://efficiency-benchmark.com/. We have made significant improvements to the original benchmark paper [1], increasing the range of parameter reductions possible with Teacher-Student Architectures from 2 times to 50 times, while maintaining the strict constraint of maintaining performance within 5% of the original network. We have applied this framework to various tasks and networks and have the models and code available for other researchers to build upon. Bucket Elimination is a fundamental algorithm in graphical models that enables efficient inference and optimization by breaking down a problem into a set of sub-problems, which are then solved recursively and combined. However, the original Bucket Elimination formulation suffers from a limitation where variables must be defined in a specific order, constraining the flexibility of variable ordering. In response to this restriction, we introduce a Variational Bucket Elimination approach that leverages a message-passing mechanism and a potential function, allowing variables to be defined arbitrarily without the need for a fixed order. By separating variable definition from elimination, our method unlocks the ability to combine sub-problems from different variable orderings, thereby facilitating an exchange of useful information and improving the accuracy of inferred values and the efficiency of computation. From a different perspective, Variational Bucket Elimination can be viewed as a generalization of the Variational Sum-Product algorithm, with potential applications extending beyond Buck Elimination to a broader range of messaging architectures. We provide a detailed analysis of Variational Bucket Elimination, including a theoretical framework for assessing the quality of inferred values, as well as experimental results demonstrating the benefits of this method in comparison to established techniques. In particular, we observe that Variational Bucket Elimination yields superior performance in tasks such as inference, optimization, and clustering, across various benchmark datasets and scenarios. In addition, we offer an open-source implementation of Variational Bucket Elimination to facilitate further research and practical applications. In summary, Variational Bucket Elimination is a versatile and adaptable algorithm that empowers users to tackle a wide range of graphical model tasks and problems. The precise influence of photon recoil on the light beam's shape relies on the density of the medium and can be compared to other effects that are typically more significant but become smaller than the one caused by photon recoil in very dense media. Public sector professionals rely heavily on Web search results when making decisions. It is crucial they are aware that Web search algorithms prioritize certain content over other relevant information, potentially leading to algorithmic bias in their decision-making. This paper investigates the extent to which Web search results reflect the diverse needs of their users. It examines the search results provided by Google, Bing, and Yahoo for 100 distinct public sector search queries, focusing on the visibility of results based on gender, ethnicity, age, and profession. The analysis reveals significant variations in search result diversity. For example, searches related to gender often yield results biased towards female perspectives, while searches related to ethnicity often yield results biased towards minority ethnic groups. However, searches related to age frequently produce results biased towards older adults. The paper also explores the impact of using Google's custom search engine for the UK Government website. The results show that this search engine prioritizes results from the National Health Service (NHS) and Gov.uk, but produces results that are less diverse than Google searches for the same queries. The paper concludes with recommendations for improving the diversity of Web search results, particularly for public sector contexts. It suggests that search engines could be incentivized to increase result diversity by making the underlying algorithms transparent and accountable. The paper also recommends that custom search engines be tested for bias before being adopted by public sector organizations. Finally, it advises professionals in the public sector to be mindful of algorithmic bias in Web search results and to use search engines that provide the most diverse results for their needs. The paper's findings and its research method are suitable for students conducting similar studies in the future. The paired-permutation test is a statistical method used to analyze the differences between two groups of measurements. This test's efficiency can be enhanced with the development of an exact algorithm, which is now superior to the Monte Carlo approximation. The new exact algorithm takes advantage of a recent efficient all-paths algorithm from graph theory. By leveraging this algorithm, the paired-permutation test can be performed exactly for the first time on a large-scale dataset with hundreds of data points. Our studies reveal that the new exact algorithm outperforms the Monte Carlo approximation, achieving a significant speed-up of ten thousand times for large datasets. Furthermore, the paired-permutation test can be extended to a non-paired version of the test. Our implementation of the paired-permutation test is an openly available Python package called PermuteTest. It provides a user-friendly interface for conducting the paired-permutation test and has been applied successfully to the analysis of certain biomedical images. Our work paves the way for the widespread use of the paired-permutation test in various fields beyond neuroscience. Our code is applicable to both paired and non-paired tests and can be downloaded from the code repository of PermuteTest on GitHub. The US shipping industry is known to be heavily influenced by cartels formed by shipping companies, which control freight rates for specific routes by limiting ship supplies. In 2012, the US and European antitrust authorities imposed fines totaling $343 million on six shipping companies for violating antitrust laws and destroying documents as a result. Following the collapse of these cartels, we observed increased shipping quantities and lower freight rates in the two most critical shipping routes, the Asia-to-Westcoast and the Asia-to-US Gulf Coast routes. Our research reveals that shipping companies genuinely altered their behavior in response to reduced antitrust enforcement, rather than simply adjusting expectations of future enforcement. Furthermore, we discovered that shipping companies destroyed documents to delay rather than avoid paying fines, and that document destruction resulted in higher fines but didn't significantly impact shipping behavior. Ultimately, our study finds that shipping companies prioritize profits over antitrust compliance and will destroy documents to maintain a shipping monopoly. We also discovered that shipping companies can maintain a shipping monopoly for up to three years following the initial reduction in antitrust enforcement, and that this leads to prolonged negative impacts on consumers. Our research suggests that shipping companies will engage in document destruction to delay rather than avoid paying fines in other industries as well. We have developed a method to estimate shipping company profits with the knowledge that shipping companies typically maintain a shipping monopoly for up to three years following the initial reduction in antitrust enforcement, which enables us to calculate the negative impact of document destruction on consumer welfare. We estimate that document destruction enabled by document shredding technologies can reduce consumer welfare by up to 5 percent in the two most critical shipping routes for up to three years following the initial reduction in antitrust enforcement. We have applied this method to a range of different shipping routes and found that the negative impact of document destruction on consumer welfare can range from 1 to 15 percent. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating shellable and chordal graphs. In this context, we demonstrate that a specific type of triangulation, characterized by its association with the vertices, edges, and faces of loom spaces, is both upper and lower triangulations. Our proof expands on this insight to show that the triangulations that result from loom spaces possess both upper and lower properties, implying they can be classified as essential triangulations. Additionally, we establish a direct relationship between the 1-skein complex of a loom space and its associated triangulation, enabling us to investigate the topological properties of loom spaces. A key observation arising from this analysis is the presence of a non-trivial Alexander dual relationship between the ideal powers of the loop edges in the 1-skein complex and the faces of the triangulation. Our study also explores the connection between loom spaces and another important concept known as discrete contact structures. By extending our initial analysis to these structures, we discover that the set of their Reeb component edges corresponds to a loom space, thereby yielding a meaningful interpretation of the topological properties encoded within these structures. Our investigation into this connection further enables us to establish a significant generalization of the property shared by shellable and chordal graphs, wherein we demonstrate that the set of their cliques also defines a loom space. Our research expands upon the known results by providing a precise characterization of the topological properties represented by the set of a graph's cliques. We conclude by reviewing the relationship between loom spaces and other fundamental concepts, including their association with upper and lower triangulations, the 1-skein complex, discrete contact structures, and the topological properties of their embedded components. Our study offers a unifying framework that incorporates and builds upon these interconnected ideas and generalizes several key properties specifically attributed to shellable and chordal graphs. Our results also reveal that the most reliable indicators vary greatly from one stock to another, highlighting the potential for a tailored approach in this domain. This research investigates the Higgs Effective Field Theory's (HEFT) double Higgs boson production in the Large Hadron Collider, comparing it to the Standard Model Effective Field Theory's (SMEFT). To do this, we considered the most significant contributors to double Higgs production in both HEFT and SMEFT, then developed a fitting framework that connects the two theories based on their common low-energy implications. By doing this, we connected the HEFT's and SMEFT's parameters in the double Higgs scenario, establishing a direct relationship between the two sets of parameters. This allowed us to translate the LHC's double Higgs boson production constraints into both HEFT and SMEFT, and demonstrate that future LHC Higgs studies can be easily adapted to both effective field theories. Additionally, we analyzed the future prospects of exploring the HEFT and SMEFT in the double Higgs channel at the High Energy LHC and Future Circular Colliders. This research demonstrated that the HEFT can be distinguished from the SMEFT through double Higgs boson production at the LHC, and that the HEFT's anomalous coupling distribution can be identified at the LHC and Future Circular Colliders. This discovery will be possible at the High Energy LHC with 3 ab−1 of data or the Future Circular Collider with 5 ab−1 of data. This research also highlighted the future possibilities of investigating the HEFT and SMEFT at the LHC and Future Circular Colliders in the double Higgs boson production channel. This involves studying the double Higgs boson production processes HH and HHH in the HEFT and SMEFT at the LHC and Future Circular Colliders. This research demonstrated that the LHC with 3 ab−1 of data or the Future Circular Collider with 5 ab−1 of data can constrain the HEFT's and SMEFT's new physics scales from double Higgs boson production to be as low as 20 TeV. This research also highlighted the necessity of incorporating Higgs self-coupling effects into the SMEFT to accurately analyze the double Higgs boson production processes HH and HHH in the SMEFT at the LHC and Future Circular Colliders. This will be crucial for uncovering the mechanisms underlying Higgs boson interactions beyond the Standard Model in the double Higgs boson production channel at the LHC and Future Circular Colliders. We investigated the drag experienced by a cylindrical solid moving through a granular bed that is driven by vibrations. The cylindrical solid moved parallel to its long axis within a two-dimensional granular sheet that was subjected to vertical vibrations. Experiments were conducted over a wide range of speeds and were characterized by the presence of drag forces acting on the solid and forces lifting the solid upwards. The strength of the drag forces varied significantly depending on the speed at which the solid was moved and exhibited peaks at certain speeds. The peaks in drag force were found to be caused by the stickiness of the granular material to the solid and occurred when the speed at which the solid was moved was lower than the speed at which the solid sank into the granular bed. The strength of the drag forces also increased with the speed at which the solid was moved when the speed was higher than the speed at which the solid sank into the granular bed. The strength of the drag forces was found to be influenced by the speed at which the solid was moved and the speed at which the granular bed was driven, and was found to be determined by the difference between these two speeds when the difference was small. When the difference between the speeds was large, the strength of the drag forces was found to be determined by the speed at which the solid was moved rather than the speed at which the granular bed was driven. The strength of the drag forces also increased with the difference between the speeds at which the solid was moved and the granular bed was driven when the difference was large. The cylindrical solid was found to sink into the granular bed when the speed at which it was moved was higher than the speed at which the granular bed was driven, and the depth to which the solid sank increased with the difference between the speeds at which it was moved and the granular bed was driven. The time it took for the solid to move a certain distance through the granular bed also increased with the difference between the speeds at which it was moved and the granular bed was driven. The strength of the drag forces was found to be influenced by the ratio of the diameter of the cylindrical solid to the size of the granular material and increased with this ratio. Notably, the ratios of $v_3$ to $v_2$ are found to be remarkably constant across different transverse momentum ranges, spanning from 0.4 GeV/c to 5 GeV/c. To further elucidate this similarity, we compared it to corresponding ratios observed in proton-proton collisions at the same collision energy, finding them to be significantly larger for both light and heavy identified particles. Furthermore, our research indicates that the triangular and elliptic flow ratios can be accurately described by a single universal function that is independent of particle type, demonstrating that the similarity between $v_3$ and $v_2$ ultimately stems from the identical radial flow patterns exhibited by all particles and scattering projectiles off each other. Additionally, we successfully simulated these phenomena using a hydrodynamical model of heavy-ion collisions. This study offers first-time evidence of a universal relationship between triangular and elliptic flow that can be interpreted through a radical flow scenario, and provides a significant insight into the basic physics governing heavy-ion collisions. The universal nature of this phenomenon is anticipated to hold true for all collision energies studied, and it is expected to serve as a key reference for future comparisons at lower collision energies. The underlying mechanisms responsible for this behavior have been conclusively identified through simulations conducted as part of this research. The findings regarding the universal ratio of $v_3$ to $v_2$ also demonstrate that heavy-ion collisions are governed by radial flow patterns rather than impact parameters. The similarities observed in the transverse momentum dependencies of $v_3$ and $v_2$ from the ALICE experiment have been successfully reproduced through the hydrodynamical model of heavy-ion collisions. The research has also led to the development of a new universal function that describes the ratios of $v_3$ to $v_2$ across different transverse momentum ranges, representing a significant contribution to the existing body of knowledge on heavy-ion collisions. The proposed modified FGMRES algorithm introduces a significant improvement to the standard FGMRES iteration by incorporating an additional term into its residual formulation. This modification aims to enhance the convergence properties of the FGMRES method, particularly in situations with ill-conditioned matrices. The analysis of the modified GMRGES algorithm is explored in detail. Theoretical convergence proofs are provided for both the original and modified FGMRES algorithms in the presence of preconditioning. The effectiveness of the proposed modification is demonstrated through numerical examples presented in the paper. These examples illustrate the advantages of the modified FGMRES algorithm in achieving superior convergence compared to the standard FGMRES method for a range of linear systems with different types of matrices. The results show that the modified FGMRES algorithm consistently outperforms the standard FGMRES algorithm for both complex and real-valued linear systems. The proposed modification can be applied to both non-Hermitian and Hermitian positive-definite linear systems. The paper also presents a MATLAB implementation of the modified FGMRES algorithm. The code is accompanied by example use cases that include the solution of continuous and discrete Helmholtz problems. The performance of the modified FGMRES algorithm is compared to the standard FGMRES algorithm for these examples. The results show that the modified FGMRES algorithm achieves better convergence than the standard FGMRES algorithm for all the examples tested. The paper also explores the relationship between the proposed modification and existing FGMRES variants, including the harmonic FGMRES algorithm. The proposed modification is found to be a special case of the harmonic FGMRES algorithm with specific parameter settings. The paper provides the source code for the modified FGMRES algorithm and example use cases that can be downloaded from the following link: https://github.com/ying-2019/MFGMRES. Accurate organ modeling through registration is crucial for enhancing surgical outcomes, but the introduction of noise in intraoperative data can impede this process. This study tackles the challenge of modeling lung anatomy during surgery, where noise in intraoperative data leads to misalignment of pre-surgical constructs with patient data. To address this, we developed a novel approach that combines a registration algorithm with a differential evolution-based optimization method to obtain optimized solutions. Furthermore, we introduced a constraint to restrict the search space for solutions, which significantly reduced computing time. The effectiveness of our proposed framework was demonstrated through simulations of lung surgery, where it successfully modeled 75% of lung anatomy with an average distance error of 5mm/10mm within noise levels of 5mm/10mm. These results showed that our approach can efficiently register noisy intraoperative data with lung models by adapting the LDDP algorithm, and this framework has the potential for application in other organ types. Estimating optical flow is a fundamental and challenging task, especially when relying on self-supervised methods. Our investigation focuses on a critical issue that affects the consistency of optical flow across neighboring frames, specifically how it behaves in the presence of occlusions. To address this, we develop a novel, two-stage approach, initially determining probable occlusion regions and subsequently using them to direct the flow estimation network. Our proposed method leverages a contrastive learning technique to establish a contrast between spatially transformed neighboring frames, effectively differentiating actual from imaginary occlusions. This results in a dedicated map indicating probable occlusion areas, which in turn is integrated into the flow estimation network, facilitating the estimation of consistent flow across neighboring frames. Our evaluations using the MPI-SAI and KITTI datasets reveal our approach to yield flow estimates that compare favorably to the current state-of-the-art methods in both metrics, C-alpha and EPE. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyun113/sdf-flow. Our research confirms the efficacy of our method in reducing the number of incorrect pixels designated as occlusions by self-supervised flow estimation networks, which we quantify as a 12.43% reduction in the MPI-SAI dataset. Our proposed technique has the added benefit of facilitating the development of robust flow estimation networks in the presence of occlusions, which we demonstrate through experiments designed to manipulate the spatiotemporal consistency of both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our approach provides a meaningful contribution to the consistency of flow estimation in the presence of occlusions, which remains a challenging and unresolved issue to date. A simple, low-power memory-based neural network is proposed, consisting of a single layer with multiple outputs, which categorizes input data into different classes. By leveraging the fundamental properties of a spike-based neural system, this model's energy efficiency is shown to significantly surpass that of conventional ANNs. Through an appropriately designed training program, this memory-based network is capable of matching the classification performance of its traditional ANNs counterparts. As an example, it is demonstrated that this model can classify handwritten numbers (MNIST) with an accuracy of 98.85%, outperforming a comparable small-scale ANNs with a 99.37% success rate in a randomized trial. As another example, with a 90.01% success rate in a randomized trial, it is shown that this model can identify tumor types (BC Cancer) from genetic data with the same precision as a more complex ANNs. This model's advantages are attributed to its minimized parameter count and it has potential applications in machine learning on wearable devices and similar platforms with limited processing power. A basic version of this model can be used as a building block for more complex memory-based networks that combine multiple layers to tackle more intricate problems. A key issue in time-domain full waveform inversion (FWI) is the emergence of noise in model estimates, particularly during the early stages of the inversion process. We introduce a new strategy, time-domain phase inversion (TDPI), which leverages the advantages of both FWI and eikonal waveform inversion. Specifically, we use the eikonal solver from the latter to mitigate the challenges associated with using time-domain wavefields. This new method is a direct extension of the ideas underlying the polarized BFGS algorithm, with the addition of a line search procedure and a polynomial interpolation technique to ensure convergence. We address the issue of updating the slowness model in time-domain simulations by the source term, which can result in nonphysical models. To mitigate this, we employ the polarized BFGS algorithm with a line search and a minimum model condition. We also introduce a new strategy to update the source term in time-domain simulations, which we refer to as the'residual method'. This new method is a direct extension of the ideas underlying the polarized BFGS algorithm, with the addition of a line search procedure and a polynomial interpolation technique to ensure convergence. We validate the accuracy and robustness of TDPI by means of synthetic data generated using the acoustic wave equation solver SANGEM, and compare the results with those obtained using the standard BFGS algorithm. We also examine the effectiveness of the residual method in updating the source term in time-domain simulations. Additionally, we apply TDPI to real data from an offshore seismic survey in the North Sea, using the same acoustic wave equation solver used for the synthetic data examples. We compare the resulting velocity models with those obtained using the standard BFGS algorithm, and investigate the differences between them. We also examine the relationship between the model update and the source term in time-domain simulations. Finally, we highlight the potential limitations of TDPI and propose potential future work, including the extension of this new strategy to frequency-domain FWI and the development of more robust methods for updating the source term in time-domain simulations. We also propose the use of multiple polarization algorithms to update the slowness model in time-domain simulations, and the use of the residual method in time-domain simulations in the presence of nonlinear elastic effects. An asymmetric noisy voter model is described as follows: at each time step, one of two species, denoted by the variables $\sigma_i(t)$ and $\sigma_j(t)$, are chosen at random to switch with a probability $p$, or to adopt one of the other species with probabilities $1-p$ that are proportional to their current population. This model is applied to a random regular graph with $N$ nodes connected to $k=\omega(\sqrt{N})$ neighbors, and we investigate the long-term dynamics of this model for an infinite number of time steps. It is shown that for $p<1$, there are three possible outcomes: one species will become extinct, the population will be evenly split between the two species, or one species will dominate the other by a margin of at least $1-pol(N)$. The conditions under which each of these three outcomes occur are also established, and these conditions are sensitive to the value of $p$. When $p=1$, the model becomes the noisy voter model, which can result in the simultaneous coexistence of the two species or their competition leading to one species' extinction. In contrast, the asymmetric noisy voter model can exhibit the coexistence of the two species for an infinite number of time steps when $p=1$, provided that the population of the species remains marginally uneven. In addition, the conditional expectation time until one species becomes extinct in the asymmetric noisy voter model can increase exponentially with the number of time steps, in contrast to a power relationship observed in the noisy voter model. The relationship between the expected time until one species becomes extinct and the number of time steps in the asymmetric noisy voter model involves the variable $p$ raised to the power of minus the number of time steps. To gain a deeper understanding of how languages evolve, it's necessary to unpack complex semantic changes. Previous studies have identified potential factors influencing these changes, but they generally vary independently of the surrounding language. We introduce a way to reexamine semantic shifts considering the broader linguistic context, using a measure of variance that captures how related words' meanings relate to each other. We discover that variations in contextual variance can either be non-paired or paired, and by considering both the changed word and its surrounding context as a whole, we find that many previous conclusions actually represent combined changes in both the word and its context. Our analysis also reveals that variations in variance can result in both the narrowing and broadening of a word's meaning, contradicting previous findings that the latter is more common. We further investigate the interplay between changes in variance and other factors like frequency and category structure. Our findings demonstrate that the interplay between these factors is more complex than initially thought, necessitating a more nuanced understanding of how languages evolve over time. We conclude that the way we describe semantic changes must be more precise, taking into account the varied contexts in which words are used, and we propose potential avenues for exploring the dynamics of category structure in relation to context. Our analysis is underpinned by 31 diverse languages, with data spanning 10 years, covering more than 30 million text instances. Our research has significant implications for any model seeking to capture the intricacies of semantic change, and we make our code and data openly available for further study. Understanding the intricate processes of retinal development is made more complex by the dynamic nature of cell migration. A key aspect of this process is the movement of nuclei across the retina, which can be visualized through the use of a nuclear distribution metric. Although previous research has demonstrated the feasibility of this approach, a major shortcoming existed in existing algorithms - they failed to consider the spatial dynamics of nuclei during the retinal development process. To address this limitation, a novel approach was developed that leveraged a free parameter to match the distribution of nuclei across the retina, which was coupled with a second model that replicated the spatial dynamics of nuclei during the retinal development process. By applying this approach to a previously analyzed dataset, the distribution of nuclei across the retina was successfully matched and the underlying retinal development process was accurately represented, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in understanding the complex processes of retinal development. Furthermore, this approach provided new insights into the retinal development process, which included the discovery that the retinal development process is composed of multiple distinct cell migration patterns that occur in different regions of the retina, and which exhibit a non-uniform speed and direction. Additionally, this approach revealed that the retinal development process is a highly scalable process that can be accurately represented through the simulation of a small retinal sample. Furthermore, this approach was found to be robust in the presence of random variations in the distribution of nuclei across the retina. A major limitation of this approach existed in the form of a long computation time required for the simulation of a retinal development process. However, the development of more efficient algorithms through the utilization of a novel approach that combined a free parameter with a sparse grid method resulted in a significant computation time reduction of approximately two orders of magnitude, which enabled the simulation of larger retinal development processes in a computationally efficient manner. This development also enabled the creation of a user-friendly graphical user interface that allowed users to easily customize the simulation of a retinal development process by adjusting various free parameter settings. A major application of this approach existed in the form of improved retinal development process models that could be utilized in the context of vision loss disorders such as retinitis pigmentosa. Although the utilization of a free parameter provided a high degree of customization to the retinal development process model, it also resulted in a model that was less accurate in the prediction of the spatial distribution of nuclei across the retina in comparison to a model that did not incorporate a free parameter. However, this trade-off was found to be acceptable in the context of vision loss disorders

Recent close-quarters interactions between infected and uninfected individuals in settings like public transport systems, at conventions, and within fully enclosed spaces prompt the examination of super-spreader events through a new lens. These events can result in substantial increases in the transmission rate within enclosed environments and may significantly impact the dynamics of infections. To better understand this phenomenon, we developed a mathematical model that incorporates the effects of ventilation systems on the spread of the infection. By comparing this model to standard epidemiological models, we found that it exhibits more rapid disease transmission, but with a decreased number of transmissions over time. Furthermore, we present the results of simulations that reflect the rapid initial transmission observed in super-spreader events. The code used for these simulations is now openly accessible and can be easily modified to accommodate various ventilation configurations. The model we presented can be applied to a wide range of infections transmitted through the air, and it provides a mathematical framework for evaluating the effectiveness of different ventilation systems in reducing transmission. The data and computational tools are available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/ourresearch/2021-nCov-air. The current version of the code includes simulations based on previously published studies of the transmission of Seasonal Influenza, SARS, MERS, and COVID-19. This note aims to explore several codisciclicity criteria for $C_0$-semigroups consisting of operators from $L(X)$. Specifically, we will examine the conditions under which a codiscient subspace is characteristic for the set of operators that are not part of the central subspace generated by the semigroup. This investigation includes studying both regular and extended cases. Our study also delves into the properties of the Riesz spectral measure associated with the Laplace transform of the semigroup, as well as the characteristic function associated with this measure. Ultimately, our results provide codisciclicity criteria that are equivalent to those proposed by G. Greiner, with the added benefit of being more general. Furthermore, we will discuss the relationship between these criteria and those presented by extending the results obtained by J. Prüss to the case of extended codisciclicity. To enhance the precision of magnetic field measurements, global vector magnetic field maps from various solstitial periods are being developed. The success of these maps relies on accurately estimating the magnetic field at local scales. For this purpose, we evaluate the effectiveness of two approaches for estimating the fill fraction of magnetic fields from spectroscopic measurements using the Amtrac instrument. Initially, we assessed the fill fraction of magnetic fields by averaging 180-degree map segments at both poles. This method yielded reliable results but was limited to solstitial periods. To improve this, we analyzed 360-degree map segments at both poles and accounted for the difference in pixel coverage at the poles. This led to a more precise estimation of fill fraction, especially during equinoxial periods. We compared both methods to the results of direct measurements from in-situ magnetic field sensors on board the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph and found that the second approach provided more accurate results, with a standard deviation of 1.35 Gamma units compared to 1.83 for the first method. The accuracy of the second approach was further validated using data from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph at different latitude ranges and during various solar activity levels. The results showed that the fill fraction estimation method is effective across different solar conditions and can be used to estimate local magnetic fields from global map segments. The approach also demonstrated minimal bias, with a mean of -0.03 Gamma units, and was recommended for use in estimating fill fraction in future solar observations. The accuracy of the approach was attributed to the high spatial resolution of the Amtrac instrument and its ability to capture small-scale magnetic field structures. The effectiveness of this approach will depend on the spatial resolution of future solar observation instruments. The approach can be used to enhance the precision of magnetic field estimates in vector magnetic field maps by explicitly accounting for the fill fraction of magnetic fields, which is critical for accurately estimating local magnetic fields, particularly in regions with low magnetic field strengths. The standard approach to estimating fill fraction led to an overestimation of the magnetic field at low latitude regions, with an underestimation of 2.5 Gamma units at 5 Gamma units. In contrast, the second approach resulted in a smaller underestimation of 1 Gamma unit at the same latitude range. Hyperparameter optimization is crucial for enhancing the performance of supervised learning algorithms, and advanced methods like evolutionary and probability-based techniques have shown significant effectiveness. Nonetheless, these methods are not suitable for tasks involving private data, such as remote training, where the dataset cannot be accessible locally. In such cases, traditional grid search is the only viable option due to its completely remote and data-private nature. However, this approach becomes inefficient as the number of hyperparameters to be tuned increases, largely because it entails numerous remote computations, thus necessitating the development of a new, specially designed algorithm that is both remotely executable and data private. This paper presents a novel, probabilistic evolutionary algorithm called EGO-Tune, which leverages building block theory to diminish the computational burden by approximately 90% compared to traditional grid search through the remote evaluation of the most informative candidate hyperparameters. Experimental results, encompassing 12 datasets from various domains, indicate that EGO-Tune excels in terms of efficiency, accuracy, and robustness, thereby offering a superior, general-purpose solution for hyperparameter optimization in settings involving private datasets. Moreover, the paper provides an open-source implementation of EGO-Tune along with an interactive web-based interface to facilitate widespread adoption. This research has far-reaching implications for remote training tasks, particularly those involving massive datasets and complex machine learning models, where the development of more efficient hyperparameter optimization techniques is increasingly vital. We develop a social diffusion model that incorporates both spatial and temporal elements to analyze the spread of rumors. By examining the effects of precursor features and location information on the peak and attenuation coefficients of rumors, our research provides insights into their impact. Furthermore, we propose an novel indicator, the duration coefficient, to investigate the influence of these factors on the time required for rumors to die out. We validate our model using real data from the Beijing area during the 2008 SARS outbreak. Our findings indicate that location information has a greater impact on the peak coefficient of rumors than the feature of precursors do. Additionally, we discover that location information and precursor features both contribute to the attenuation and duration coefficients of rumors. Our analysis reveals that the most reliable spreader information tends to result in a shorter time for rumors to reach their peak and to die out. In contrast, the influence of dissenter information is opposite, as it leads to a longer time for rumors to peak and to attenuate. We also observe that the most trustworthy precursor information exerts a more significant influence on the attenuation coefficient of rumors than the feature of spreader information does. Our research may be utilized to create strategies for rumor mitigation and control. We propose multiple possible control scenarios and analyze their effectiveness. We present LifeStream, a high-performance streaming matrix function library for single-program, single-data architectures, including CPU and GPU platforms. LifeStream achieves superior performance, surpassing hand-optimized numerical libraries, including VSL on x86-64 and cuCBLAS on NVIDIA V100, in various applications, such as kernel methods, graph signals, and streaming linear transforms, across diverse real-world datasets. The library's versatility allows for flexible input/output data formats and supports both dense and sparse matrices, further cementing LifeStream's status as a versatile and high-performing matrix function ecosystem. We have publicly available the library's source code along with comprehensive benchmarks, showcasing its performance benefits. Given the broad utility of matrix functions across computational tasks, LifeStream is a valuable contribution to the high-performance numerical computing community, showcasing the efficacy of automatic optimization for real-world datasets and cementing streaming matrix functions as a benchmark for future developments. The source code, benchmarks, and example applications are all openly accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/mit-hpc/LifeStream. The library has been successfully used to calculate the Nyström approximation of large-scale kernel matrices, demonstrating significant performance gains in comparison to established methods, including a 5.8-fold speedup when applying the kernel perceptron to SIFT data comprising one million training images. As such, LifeStream is a cutting-edge, widely applicable matrix function library poised to serve as a benchmark for the further improvement of automatic optimization techniques. The underlying LifeStream framework has also been utilized to develop a high-performance, streaming Nystrom approximation algorithm referred to as LifeStream-Nystrom, which the authors propose as a novel, efficient method for handling large-scale kernel machines. Unlike conventional Nystrom approximations that focus on selecting random sample points, LifeStream-Nystrom leverages the streaming matrix function library to construct a weighted sample set where the weights are directly derived from the original kernel matrix, resulting in a precise match between the original and approximate distributions as measured by the Wasserstein distance. Consequently, LifeStream-Nystrom is shown to yield superior performance, achieving a 2.8-fold speedup and a 2.5-fold reduction in approximation error when applied to the kernel SVM on SIFT data comprising one million training images, in comparison to state-of-the-art methods, such as buck stream Nystrom and sparse Nystrom, which themselves represent optimized variants of the basic Nystrom approximation algorithm. Magnetic susceptibility in superconducting materials can be influenced by the topology of their Fermi surfaces. To understand this interplay, we develop a general framework for calculating the magnetic susceptibility in the presence of spin--orbit coupling, using a parametrization of Fermi surface contours derived from DFT simulations. We then apply this method to search for a possible nematic superconducting state in Nb3Sf, considering the verified electronic structure and possible scenarios for the interplay between magnetic and electronic properties. By comparing our results with experimentally determined neutron scattering data, we analyze the conditions under which the nematic superconducting state or the magnetic susceptibility can be realized. Moreover, we investigate the effects of the 121 component of the s--wave pairing symmetry on the magnetic susceptibility, and by combining this with the earlier mentioned considerations, we propose a theoretical explanation for the spatially varying nematic susceptibility observed in Nb3Sf. We also explore the impact of the 121 component of the s--wave pairing on the energy spectra of quasiparticles in this material. By modeling quasiparticle energy spectra with varying magnetic moment directions, we can explain the observed fluctuations of the 121 component of the s--wave pairing in Nb3Sf. This method is based on an analogy between the Euler-Lagrange equation and the Van Hove hydrodynamic equation, leading to a diffusion equation that predicts the time it takes for the system to reach equilibrium. This prediction is independent of the system's initial conditions and is therefore a true invariant. However, the validity of this result depends on the condition that the system's fluctuations are small and the system remains in the grand canonical ensemble, with pressures closely spaced. A new approach is developed here to calculate the thermodynamic properties of the system at constant pressure, without relying on the distance between pressures. This new approach involves a Fokker-Planck equation with a diffusion coefficient that varies with pressure, allowing the derivation of a scaling relationship between the compressibility and the equilibrium properties of the system. This model is tested against molecular dynamics simulations of Lennard-Jones fluids with different particle densities. The results show that the compressibility of these systems follows the predicted scaling laws, even when the systems are far from equilibrium and there are significant differences in pressure. The benefits of this approach are also demonstrated by the fact that the equation of state of these systems can be obtained through the scaling relationship, without the need for the knowledge of the initial conditions or the distance between pressures. The applicability of this approach is not limited to Lennard-Jones fluids, as it is expected to be universally applicable to any class of fluids with short-range interactions. The advantages of this method are particularly evident when the systems under study have long periods of time or large spatial distances to reach equilibrium. We investigate the asymptotic properties of the first k_n parking places, denoted as X_{(1)}, X_{(2)}... X_{(k_n)}, where X_i represents the location where the i-th car is parked. We establish central limit theorems for the normalized version of these ordered locations, and also examine their variation distance and Kolmogorov distance as parking places increase. In particular, we find that the variation distance and Kolmogorov distance between the classical uniform distribution on [0,1] and the distribution of the first k_n parking places are both asymptotically equal to $\sqrt{k_n}/(k_n+1)$. Additionally, we derive an asymptotic expression for the Kolmogorov distance per unit length. We further develop these results by considering the parking problem with an exclusion zone, which involves preventing cars from parking in certain defined areas. In this variant, we show that the distribution of the first k_n parking places converges to a non-trivial limit, with this limit being governed by a continuous time stochastic process, with the advantage that this process can be numerically computed efficiently. We also establish that the variation distance and Kolmogorov distance between the original and modified distributions of the first k_n parking places both converge to a value asymptotically proportional to $1/(k_n+1)$. We validate the practical applicability of these results by employing them in the context of a statistical test used in the analysis of temporal patterns in activity data. This test relies on the distribution of the first k_n parking places, which allows us to outline the steps for conducting the test and obtaining its statistical power. We leverage previous knowledge of uniform distributions as a starting point, with specific adjustments to cater to the aspects of activity data that exhibit little structure beyond excluding certain defined areas. We appraise the impact of excluding specific areas on the variation distance and Kolmogorov distance of the first k_n parking places. We explore various shapes that can be used to define these excluded areas, which we term "masks". We establish that the variation distance and Kolmogorov distance of the first k_n parking places are both asymptotically equal to the area of the mask divided by the total area, which we denote as the "exclusion ratio". We also examine the suitability of different mask shapes, including squares, circles, and truncated triangles, with the goal of identifying the most efficient mask shape in terms of the area required to achieve a specified variation distance

A key component in quantum photonic networks is the beam splitter, which relies on precise control of both low-order and higher-order optical modes. In an effort to address scaling limitations of classical algorithms for quantum simulation, we investigate a phase beam splitter driven by a single parameter, with the aim of generalizing its functionality to multiple optical modes while preserving mode-matching accuracy. Utilizing the Jones and Mueller matrix formalisms, we derive an explicit expression for the phase beam splitter's transfer function, which can be implemented using a single optical phase modulator. To demonstrate the validity of this approach, we conduct an optical demonstration of a single-parameter beam splitter, successfully applying it to the reconstruction of higher-order photonic modes. Furthermore, our work paves the way for a universal phase beam splitter capable of processing multi-degree optical modes. Our findings are validated by an optical demonstration of a single-parameter beam splitter, including the reconstruction of higher-order photonic modes. Our work paves the way for a universal phase beam splitter capable of processing multi-degree optical modes, offering a crucial step towards efficient quantum simulation with large-scale, complex systems. We propose an optical implementation based on a single parameter beam splitter, which can be realized using a 4-f system and a phase modulator, and successfully demonstrate this concept using a 40 GHz LiNbO3 phase modulator and a mode-locked laser, successfully reconstructing an optical mode with up to 5 degrees of freedom. Our approach provides a crucial step towards efficient quantum simulation with large-scale, complex systems. We propose an optical implementation based on a 4-f system and a phase modulator, and successfully demonstrate this concept using a 40 GHz LiNbO3 phase modulator and a mode-locked laser, successfully reconstructing an optical mode with up to 5 degrees of freedom. Our proposed beam splitter implementation is also highly versatile, and could be used in a variety of applications, including quantum simulation, optical interferometry, and optical sensing. However, the actual process involves breaking symmetries, specifically flavor symmetry breaking and spin-symmetry breaking. This research analyzes the mass spectra of baryons, specifically meson-baryon interactions, using the quark model with instanton-induced interactions. By applying the 24-dimensional representation of instanton-induced interactions, we generate mass spectra for different baryon states, including nucleons, delta baryons, sigma baryons, lambda baryons, and omega baryons. We also examine the decay widths of instanton-induced resonances in sigma-baryon and omega-baryon mass spectra. Furthermore, this research predicts new resonances in omega-baryon mass spectra and suggests decay modes for previously unobserved omega and sigma baryons. Calculated mass differences and decay widths are compared to existing data from LHCb, FAIR, and the BNL Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). Additionally, this research predicts mass ranges and decay widths for predicted omega and sigma baryons based on quark composition. We also outline experimental searches for these predicted states of omega and sigma baryons at the above mentioned facilities. In recent years, research on the epidemiology of respiratory viruses has integrated environmental factors into its analyses. This study employs a simplified model of aerosol dynamics to explore the impact of particle interactions and other environmental influences on the spread of these viruses. Specifically, we examine how aerosol concentration affects the transmission of infectious particles, taking into account the competing processes of particle settlement and mixing. We compare this model to more complex, statistically supported descriptions of aerosol behavior in various environments, finding that it accurately captures the temporal evolution of aerosol concentrations. However, differences in model scaling reveal that it assumes shorter average lifetimes for airborne viruses (around 20 minutes) compared to estimates based on data from various locations (ranging from 16 to 63 minutes). We discuss the implications of this model for the distribution of aerosol concentrations around an infected individual and present a statistical analysis of its parameters based on data from 17 different geographical regions. We also use this model to simulate the effectiveness of various public health interventions, including the use of face masks and ventilation systems, and explore its limitations due to the simplified representation of aerosol dynamics. Ultimately, this study provides a computationally efficient model of aerosol behavior that can be applied to a broad range of epidemiological scenarios. We offer the model, along with the code used to simulate it, to the scientific community for further development and testing. This model can be used to simulate the transmission of respiratory viruses that are primarily spread through the air, including those caused by influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and tobacco smoke. This, in turn, can be used to estimate the distance over which an infectious person can spread the virus to an uninfected individual, as well as the probability of transmitting the virus through such an interaction. To better understand the scattering mechanism, we examined the Hall coefficient under applied stress in thin films of Cobalt/Bismuth. Due to the anisotropic properties of Bismuth, the Hall coefficient displayed a clear orientation dependence. Based on crystallographic analysis, we found that the Hall coefficient correlated with the  scattering off Bismuth layers rather than Cobalt layers. As a result, we were able to employ a simple model to effectively increase the carrier concentration in these multilayers, resulting in a significant decrease in the Hall coefficient and a corresponding increase in the carrier concentration. We were also able to employ the anisotropic conductivity tensor of Bismuth to further investigate the Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers. Ultimately, we were able to compare these results with an FMR-based investigation of the same samples, where the spin-lattice relaxation time obtained from FMR closely matched the Hall-effect-derived carrier concentration. Hence, we demonstrated that Bismuth layers dictate the Hall-effect scattering mechanism in these multilayers, and also established a viable technique for determining the carrier concentration in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers using the Hall effect. Nonetheless, this discovery also highlighted the potential for controlling the spin-lattice relaxation time in these materials by adjusting the applied stress. The NLO+PS generator MELA for vector leptoquarks has been enhanced by overhailing signal events with corrected NLO distributions, which addresses issues with threshold behavior and incorrect predictions seen in other generators for high invariant masses. Utilizing the Frixione-wide streaming technique facilitates efficient handling of NLO distributions, while a purposeful reordering of emissions prioritizes lepton pairs to reduce computational costs and mitigate leptonic contamination from non-diffractive backgrounds. The generator MELA, incorporated into the Delphes simulation framework, demonstrates a significant improvement in vector leptoquark searches by reducing the number of signal events incorrectly classified as background, thereby increasing the sensitivity of existing search results. The enhanced generator MELA is available for public use, along with an updated Delphes installation that includes vector leptoquark simulations for various production processes and decay channels, including pairs, single, and triple leptoquark productions, as well as leptonic decays to electrons and muons. The associated Delphes card allows for customizable simulation settings, including options for implementing NLO+PS corrections, adjusting parton shower evolution, and selecting for different leptoquark charges and masses. The MELA generator and updated Delphes simulation can be accessed through the CERN Git laboratory. This study examines how neural coreference resolution is influenced by contextualized word embeddings, specifically in the context of centering theory. Initially, we compared the performance of several coreference resolution models using BERT, which resulted in significant improvements, but we recognized the need for a more nuanced analysis. To this end, we introduced a framework for assessing the coreference patterns within a dataset and modeled them using centering theory's three categories: same, shift, and contrast. Through this framework, we observed that neural coreference resolution accurately identifies "same" coreferences but struggles with "shift" and "contrast" coreferences. Furthermore, we discovered that contextualized word embeddings exacerbate the difficulties with "shift" and "contrast" coreferences, leading to degraded performance in 51% of coreferences within these categories. We also discovered that BERT coreferences often prioritize semantic similarity over syntactic similarity. To mitigate these issues, we proposed several strategies, including utilizing a neural network to distinguish between "shift" and "same" coreferences based on encoded contextualized word embeddings, integrating a measure of syntactic relatedness into the coreference score, and leveraging a neural network to classify coreferences into "same", "shift", or "contrast" categories. Ultimately, our proposed model yielded a 5.5% F1-score improvement over the baseline BERT model. We also explored the coreferences predicted by the model that are deemed most challenging and analyzed the underlying factors contributing to these difficult cases. Our empirical results demonstrate the benefits of utilizing contextualized word embeddings with caution and integrating a deeper understanding of the coreference relation through neural networks. Our research framework and methodologies are versatile and applicable to other natural language processing tasks influenced by the coreference relations, such as sentiment analysis and part-of-speech tagging. Our code and data annotations are available for public access at https://github.com/zhuyong157/coref-ct. Our findings are significant for the coreference resolution community and provide a foundation for further research into the underlying causes of challenging coreferences and effective strategies for addressing them. As WiFi fingerprinting networks expand, there's a growing need to estimate the distance between fingerprints. Traditional metric-based methods are limited by their inability to effectively utilize additional sources of information. In contrast, machine learning approaches can leverage various inputs, but often require extensive training data, posing a challenge in large geospatial applications. This paper introduces DistSense, a novel distance estimation framework utilizing low-dimensional representation of spatial variations. It achieves this goal by training a embedding model on the fingerprint features, making it feasible to utilize WiFi fingerprints without a comprehensive training set. Experiments conducted in two separate, independent datasets demonstrate DistSense's efficacy, showing a significant improvement (by at least 50%) in estimation accuracy compared to traditional approaches. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits robust performance across changing mobility patterns and network configurations. Ultimately, DistSense facilitates a precise and adaptable distance estimation solution for large-scale WiFi fingerprint networks. This is further supported by the code and dataset available at: https://github.com/Tianming924/DistSense. Despite the proposed method's performance, it is essential to note that the accuracy of distance estimation may be compromised in areas with high network density, due to the inherent limitation of IP disambiguation. This paper is built upon the research introduced in the paper titled Sensing Geospatial Distance between WiFi Access Points with Detwin. A Network-based Approach presented at Mobihoc'20. Experiments and evaluations from the original publication are inherited in this paper for consistency. We analyze how different filling patterns affect the interplay of positive and negative beams during multiple passes and highlight how certain patterns can result in unstable beam-RF interactions, particularly when the beam is shared between multiple cells. Truncating this function at a certain value k results in a new graph, denoted as $\gamma_k$, where the geodesic distance between two vertices is limited to k edges. This study investigates the metric dimension of $\gamma_k$, establishing that it has a dimension of 1 when k is greater than 2, specifically showing that a walk of length 2 is equivalent to a path of length 3. A previous conjecture is refuted, as there is no value of k, other than 1, for which the metric dimension of $\gamma_k$ is 2. The investigation into the case of k = 1 leads to the discovery that it is possible to determine the metric dimension of $\gamma_k$ when k is less than 2, defining it as a set of vertices with a maximum geodesic distance of k from all other vertices. The resulting $\gamma_1$ metric dimension is found to be 2 for certain trees and 3 for a specific cycle, whereas it is unknown for other configurations. The investigation into $\gamma_2$ reveals that it has a metric dimension of 2 for certain trees, whereas it is unknown for other cycles. The study concludes by outlining an algorithm to calculate the metric dimension of $\gamma_k$, specifically for a given tree with a maximum geodesic distance of 2, by first determining the number of branches and then identifying a minimum metric dimension subset. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated on various examples. The investigation into $\gamma_k$ provides a foundation for exploring similar problems involving other distance functions, offering potential applications in various domains. The algorithm developed for $\gamma_2$ has a polynomial time complexity of O(n^3), while the general algorithm for $\gamma_k$ has a time complexity of O(f(n)) for an unknown value of f(n). Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) vary significantly due to a interplay of mechanisms, making long-term behavior analysis quite challenging. Traditional techniques struggle to effectively utilize extensive observational data sets spanning decades, leading to a substantial portion of valuable information being wasted. In contrast, machine learning approaches have made considerable progress in this realm, with techniques such as reinforcement learning and neural network-based methods producing promising results. We test the capability of two prominent models, a neural network-based interpreter and a reinforcement learning agent, in accurately classifying and estimating measurements from previous observations for a sample of radio-loud AGNs. Both models exhibit skill in both tasks, with the navigator model demonstrating specific strength in managing observations contaminated by errors. We further investigate the capability of these models to predict physical parameters related to jets and their power, achieving a success rate of up to 70% with only a 20% increase in estimated measurements. These models also show the potential to be trained on smaller datasets, making them suitable for use with current large-scale surveys. We conclude that such models are well-suited for analyzing long-term behavior of radio-loud AGNs and predicting key physical parameters. We also provide an initial prediction for the jet power of J1430 together with a detailed re-analysis of its variability. We stress the necessity of incorporating position information and developing better models that can handle the non-linear relationships between physical parameters and their observations. We propose a straightforward approach to incorporate position information and offer a dataset of measured and predicted physical parameters for radio-loud AGNs. This dataset is available upon request. We also present an investigation of the capability of these models to predict the physical parameters of another radio-loud AGN, J1430, for which we obtain repeated observations over the course of twenty years with the VLA. We ultimately find that the jet power of J1430 fluctuates greatly, with a estimated power range of 1043-1045 erg/s, and estimate its total energy density in the jet to be approximately 10 times greater than its particle energy density. We re-examine the variability of J1430 in both the radio and optical bands, finding that the variability in the radio band is more pronounced than in the optical band, with a estimated peak flux range of 10-10^2 mJy and a estimated jet energy density that could be approximately 10 times greater than its radiation energy density if the variability in both bands is driven by the same mechanism. In the context of multiagent decision-making, establishing meaningful and practical metrics to assess the quality of approximate social welfare is crucial, especially when considering fair and efficient allocation methods, such as the VM-algorithm and the EDK-algorithm, which provide guaranteed approximations in exchange for reduced computational efficiency. Previous studies have made various assumptions to achieve such guarantees, yet these conditions are more representative of idealized scenarios rather than real-world applications. To bridge this gap, we introduce two novel valuation functions that, when used, can significantly improve the accuracy of approximate social welfare, even in idealized scenarios, by incorporating bipartite matchings and directed graphs, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these functions enable us to obtain the optimal approximate social welfare, achieving a 1.5 approximation factor, which represents the first guarantee to be obtained without increasing the computational complexity beyond polynomial time. Our results also build upon the earlier findings of Feinber (1969), Dubey and Vazou (1973), and Goode (2011). Additionally, we contribute a general framework that enables us to extend our valley-free condition to other settings, including an important variant where our approximation factor decreases to 1.25, thereby tightening the existing 2 approximation factor guarantee established by Goode (2011). To facilitate widespread adoption, our approaches, conditions, and associated approximations are designed with an emphasis on simplicity and efficiency, given the valued nature of the underlying domains. Ultimately, our research provides a significant advancement in approximately achieving optimal social welfare within a measurable distance from the true optimum, as defined by the Valiant-Vazou (2013) metric, while upholding the fairness and efficiency that it ensures. Our findings offer a promising foundation for further exploration and extension in the realm of approximate mechanism design. Envelopes of resolved asteroids can be analyzed using point spread function analysis techniques to determine their composition and whether they're binary asteroids. This research develops a method to apply PSF analysis to objects from wide field surveys like Pan-STARRS, which operated at a much larger distance than tight asteroid orbits and thus resolves the asteroids into multiple components. However, this increase in resolution comes with a higher noise level due to the larger distance, making binaries less visible. To counter this, the researchers developed a technique to combine images from different optical bands with different distances, effectively combining the high resolution of the more distant near-infrared images with the lower noise of the closer optical images. This technique can potentially identify binary asteroids that would otherwise be missed in wide field surveys. The approach is tested using simulated binary asteroids and a sample of real asteroids from the Pan-STARRS survey, and the results suggest it can detect asteroids with mass ratios as low as 0.01. The technique also yields mass estimates for detected binary asteroids, and these estimates agree with those obtained from other methods, including direct observations of binary asteroids that result in moon ejections, or ejecta streams around the parent body. The technique can be applied to existing wide field surveys and future surveys like LSST, which will have a detection limit similar to Pan-STARRS. The research concludes that many binary asteroids remain undiscovered in wide field surveys, and that many of these binaries will be revealed when the orbit of an asteroid is closely examined through targeted observations with a high-resolution telescope like the Hubble Space Telescope or a large ground-based telescope like the Subaru Telescope.
